utterances.text: Good morning. We commence the final submissions for the Defence. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all. Right at the outset, we are facing a minor technical problem. The interpreters from the booths have asked me to provide my notes for this closing argument so that they could better follow the argument. Therefore, may these please be distributed to the booths so I could commence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Rodic. Anything to help. Can I say as an old counsel, I'm impressed that your notes are in such an order that the booth might be able to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for the Defence's arguments and conclusions in relation to the counts that our client has been charged with, as well as in relation to all the evidence that has been presented throughout the trial, we have drafted a detailed final brief or closing argument. Therefore, my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, and I will try today as briefly as possible to put the Defence team's final arguments before the Trial Chamber and the OTP. The former Yugoslav state was established along federative lines with six republics. The territory of the SFRY was single and unified consisting of the respective territories of the socialist republics. Under its constitution, it was established that territories could not be changed without the consent of the republics, nor could the state border of the SFRY be altered without the consent of all its republics and autonomous provinces. The supreme law and act of the SFRY was its constitution, and the republican constitutions had to comply with that overall constitution as well as all of their legal enactments and documents. Contrary to the constitution of the SFRY that was then in force, the leadership of the Republic of Croatia throughout 1991 adopted a number of measures for the unconstitutional secession of the Republic of Croatia from the SFRY. Throughout that period, they were preparing to secede; namely, the party in power in Croatia which was Tudjman's Croatian Democratic Community at the time, their assessment was that in order to reach that objective, it was necessary to first clash with the Yugoslav People's Army. The former SFRY had a defence doctrine that was based on all people's defence, meaning a large number of citizens of military age who had received military training. This represented a large military force comprising mostly the various units. Under the constitution, the armed forces of the SFRY were to protect the independent sovereignty and territorial integrity of the SFRY as well as its social and political structure. The armed forces comprised the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, and Territorial Defence units, the TO. The supreme command of the armed forces of the SFRY was the Presidency of the SFRY, which -- the body represented a collective president of state in a manner of speaking. The president of this Presidency of the SFRY on behalf of the Presidency exercised command over the armed forces of the SFRY, all in compliance with the constitution and the federal laws. It is noteworthy that in the second half of 1992, the president of the Presidency was Stjepan Mesic, who was a representative of the Republic of Croatia in this collective -- my apologies, the transcript says 1992, and I said in the second half of 1991, the president was Stjepan Mesic who was a representative of the Republic of Croatia. The Defence wishes to point out how notorious it was that Mr. Mesic at the time as well as later boasted about his role in the breakdown of the SFRY, acting in his official capacity at the time. The General Staff of the JNA was the staff of the supreme command, or rather of the Presidency of the SFRY. The chief of the General Staff throughout 1991 was General Blagoje Adzic. Control and command over the armed forces were exercised by the federal secretary for National Defence. Back in 1991, Veljko Kadijevic held this position, General Veljko Kadijevic. Throughout 1991, the armed forces of the SFRY comprised two components or elements: The Yugoslav People's Army and the TO units, Territorial Defence units. The Yugoslav People's Army at the time was composed of military or army districts, land army corps, air force, and anti-aircraft defence, military naval sectors, which belonged to the navy, and joint tactical units composed of vessels and the different services, such as brigades and squads. The JNA had its bases throughout the territory of the former SFRY, as well as the Territorial Defence was also based throughout the republics and provinces. It is also noteworthy that the republics had no authority to make autonomous decisions to use the TO units for combat purposes. This was under the exclusive jurisdiction of the supreme command of the armed forces of the SFRY. Operationally and geographically, the entire territory of the SFRY as a possible theatre of war was divided roughly into four territorial units, three theatres of war for the use of land forces and one for the navy. Each of these potential theatres of war contained forces of one strategic group. These groups were referred to as military districts or army districts or armies. Back in 1991, those were the 5th Military District based in Zagreb, which covered the following territory and units: The units of the JNA and the TO in Slovenia and Croatia with the exception of the northern coastal district. The next one was the 1st Military District with headquarters in Belgrade. Territorially speaking it covered part of Croatia, it covered Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, excluding the coastal area, of course. The 3rd Military District with headquarters in Skopje covered JNA and TO units in Macedonia and the Republic of Serbia as far as the border to the 1st Military District. The territory of the Republic of Montenegro was also included there as well as the coastal area along the Adriatic coast. This comprised JNA and TO units based on the islands and on parts of the territory that conditionally could be termed the coastal area or Primorje, which is a geographical term. The whole of the navy was grouped under that heading as well as the coastal forces. The military naval districts broke down into three military naval sectors, that of Sibenik, that of Pula, and that of Boka, also known as the 9th VPS which is how we often referred to it throughout the trial and in our documents. Speaking about the 9th VPS, the Defence wishes to point out that it covered the stretch between the town of Neum and the Albanian border to the south as well as the coastal area between 5 and 25 kilometres deep inland from the coast. The area of responsibility of this military naval sector also covered the town and garrison of Trebinje. Across the territory of the SFRY, before the breakout of the war there, existed military courts. These military courts were based in Ljubljana, Zagreb, Split, Sarajevo, Belgrade, Nis, and Skopje. The military court in Split had jurisdiction over the entire military naval district; however, the court was evacuated and transferred to Tivat because they were too short-staffed to go on functioning and operating as usual since Croatian personnel had left the military court and the military naval district. Also, in the spring of 1991, the command of the military naval district was moved from Split to the forward command post on the island of Vis. The republican leadership of Croatia throughout 1991 banned their citizens from responding to mobilisation call-ups issued by the JNA. The same leadership ordered those officers and soldiers who were in the JNA to leave their units and their institutions. Many officers from the command staff of the JNA back in 1991 were Croats and Slovenes. Back in 1991, in the territory of the SFRY, there existed a number of paramilitary units representing the armed formations attached to certain political parties. Those paramilitary units were not part of the armed forces of the SFRY. The Croatian National Guards Corps was one such paramilitary formation, or rather, an army attached to a political party, the Croatian Democratic Community which was then in power and was the leading political force in Croatia at the time. Franjo Tudjman, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, at the time the president of Croatia, took a decision to officialise the status of the National Guard Corps as a military formation, military unit, which was sanctioned in late May back in Zagreb in 1991. At the same time, in 1991, the republican police forces also grew. Prior to that, in November 1990, massive amounts of illegal weapons and military equipment had been imported into Croatia from Hungary. On the 9th of January 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY issued a decree to disarm paramilitary units. However, some members of the Presidency opposed the disarmament and banning of these paramilitaries formations or units. The very fact that certain members of the Presidency, which was the supreme command of the armed forces, opposed the disarmament of paramilitary units adversely affected members of the JNA and brought about a lack of trust. The Croatian leadership in August 1991, following several rounds of fruitless negotiations, decided to block all JNA bodies and institutions that were based throughout Croatian territory. For the most part of 1991, many attacks were carried out against units and JNA units and JNA institutions. Many of the JNA soldiers and officers were killed and slaughtered throughout 1991 in a number of different Croatian towns and cities. The transcript page that I'm referring to is 4.371. The units and garrisons of the JNA that were under blockade at the time had their electricity supplies cut as well as their food supplies, their phone lines were down as well. The Presidency of the SFRY, being the supreme command, as well as the JNA demanded that the Croatian authorities lift the blockade on a number of different occasions. The Croatian side promised several times to lift the blockade; however, this never materialised. Some of the units were evacuated throughout 1991, but throughout the year, attacks against members of the JNA, their property and families continued. Under those conditions, the supreme command staff decided that certain units should be used to carry out activities which would exert pressure on the Republic of Croatia and cause them to lift the blockade of garrisons and barracks in the Republic of Croatia in which JNA were still stationed. The military leadership had several things to deal with at the same time. They had to create and put together in an operational way armed forces that were to carry out operations against paramilitary units. In late summer 1991, the military leadership saw itself compelled to start adapting the concept of strategical grouping to a newly arisen set of circumstances. That is why they began to set up so-called temporary units such as operational and tactical groups. One such temporary military formation was the 2nd Operational Group. It was established in late September 1991 and was meant to unify or unite command over elements of the 37th Corps from Uzice, elements of the 2nd Corps based in Podgorica, elements of the 4th Corps based in Sarajevo, and the 9th Military Naval Sector of Boka, or rather, the 9th VPS. Speaking in general terms about operational groups as such, we must say that these are established when extraordinary circumstances arise Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond and new operational needs must be met. These are one-off formations for special operational missions. Operational groups are usually established in special and isolated zones of operation where it is necessary to unite all combat activity carried out by a number of different units. Operational groups are mainly established in order to act along auxiliary axes and directions. Speaking of their provisional nature, that means that operational groups, after completing a task, are disbanded, but they remain active until completion of their task subject to the decision of their superior command. During the trial, we had opportunity to hear Prosecution Witness General Zorc who explained the possibilities allowing for the existence of an operational group. He explained there are several possibilities, but we are interested in only one of them; namely, the situation wherein the General Staff sets up an operational group drawing units from different military districts. An operational group can include one or several corps from different arms of service or logistical sectors of different military districts. In that case, the operational group would be led and commanded by the corresponding general and the personnel of the units combined to make up the group. Witness Zorc says that such a group would be under the direct command of the General Staff whereas the units in its composition would only be under the provisional command of its commander. Witness Zorc emphasises that the order of the superior command to set up such an operational group must include command competencies and authorisations. If command authorities were to be restricted in any way, for instance, if they were to be restricted only to operational control and decision on the engagement of units, that would have to be clearly stated in the order to set up the operational group. That is Prosecution Exhibit P204, page 7. Witness Zorc underlined during his testimony that there is no evidence before this Trial Chamber on the purview or scope of the command authority of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. In other words, he was unable to establish whether his command competencies were unlimited or restricted, and that we can find in the transcript of his testimony on page 6.569 and 6.570. The establishment of the 2nd Operational Group in 1991 did not imply that the command would be established first and come out on the location where command was supposed to emanate from with a defined zone responsibility, and only after that, bring in the units that were subordinated to it. In this case, precisely the opposite happened. The units were either already in the zone of responsibility or on their way, or alternatively, it was envisaged that they arrive there following a march. The command of the operational group arrived, and the commander of the General Staff only made public the decision to include certain units in it. The operational group did not include the entire naval forces and the land forces of the 9th VPS. Part of the forces of the 9th VPS still remained within the zone of the VPS, and the operational group included only those forces that were indispensable to reinforce the operational group in its task to impose a blockade on Dubrovnik. It strikes us immediately that only the forces of the 9th VPS were located in their native area, whereas all the other units included in the 2nd Operational Group were brought in from their original zones of responsibility and deployed in a totally unfamiliar zone of responsibility, foreign to them. The zone of responsibility of the 2nd Operational Group was in the area of eastern Herzegovina up to the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia on the one hand and Serbia-Montenegro on the other hand, up to the Neretva River on one side, and the coastal area on the other side, including the islands as well as the peninsula of Peljesac. The 2nd Operational Group was a formation on the level of an army. A command of the 2nd Operational Group at the time consisted of personnel from Belgrade and Podgorica as well as from Bileca. General Strugar by virtue of the order of the chief of General Staff dated the 12th of October 1991 was directed to work in the 2nd Operational Group for three months. While he headed the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar received his assignments directly from the General Staff, and it is noteworthy that he was the third commander to head that operational group within a very short time. There were many problems in the combat constitution of the units of this operational group. It must be said that the mobilisation took place under the auspices of a military exercise because the country was not in a state of war at the time. Under those circumstances, mobilisation was carried out almost on a voluntary principle. Not a single unit with the exception of the 9th Military Naval Sector was familiar with the zone of responsibility, in other words, the territory where it would be engaged in combat. Most of these units from the 2nd Operational Group found the territory completely alien, and that included the area where they had to move within combat operations. The mobilisation of units took place in their original zones of responsibility, the places where they came from. Reinforcement was made from areas located elsewhere in the country, and the personnel brought in was totally unfamiliar with the environment. It is important to note that the degree of training and the degree of solidarity and familiarity between troops and commanding staff as well as between commands and units was almost nil. And that, together with all the negative implications of such a state of affairs on the overall combat readiness of units, was extremely adverse. These were hastily put together units and commands, lacking training, that had never been trained for the tasks they would be carrying out and never familiarised with the territory where the combat operations would be taking place. Therefore, the 2nd Operational Group never existed before, not even in the similar let alone the same composition, which means that the personnel did not know each other at all, and the commands were unfamiliar with the units. The units placed under the command of the 2nd Operational Group had never carried out similar tasks before. Those were officers from the main inspectorate, from the centre of high military schools in Belgrade, and the reserve officers school from Bileca. All this was happening only ten days before the combat operations were to begin. It is almost mission impossible to retrain people within such a short time from teaching, command staff, or other duties to operations duties or command duties, without appropriate psychological preparation and retraining or requalification. This state of flux and the fact that the 2nd Operational Group was totally unfamiliar with the circumstances led to frequent changes in organisation and composition. We could see during the trial that resubordination and attachment or detachment of units took place almost on a daily basis. All this could not but cause the units of the 2nd Operational Group to carry out almost every operation in a different composition of units. We can only imagine the number and the size of problems caused by such a frequent turnover of personnel and change of the composition of units. These facts had an extremely adverse effect on any attempt to establish a favourable climate of command, which requires, first of all, great familiarity with the tasks and the zone of responsibility of individuals and units as well as commands; second, mutual familiarity, respect between personnel units, commands and staffs, as well as different levels of command; and third, it requires a high degree of qualification and training of units and commands for the implementation of forthcoming tasks. Speaking of the objectives and assignments of the 2nd Operational Group, they were best illustrated by the draft directive to attack, Defence Exhibit 44. According to that draft directive, the strategic role of the 2nd Operational Group was to establish operational control over the territory of eastern Herzegovina and southern Dalmatia from the Neretva River to the north up to the Adriatic Sea in the west, and up to the border between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina in the east and southeast, to make it impossible to annex Dubrovnik with its environs, with its broader area to the military forces that were preparing for armed insurgents aimed at secession of the Republic of Croatia from Yugoslavia. Also, the 2nd Operational Group was established in order to establish complete military control over the Neretva River valley; that is, downstream from Mostar. And in that connection, the assignment, the task was also to defend the area in Mostar and all the resources of the JNA in the Neretva River valley downstream from Mostar; namely, depots of military equipment in Dretelj and Gabela, and the large training centre in Caplinja. The task of the 2nd Operational Group was to disable a remilitarisation of the town of Dubrovnik and to prevent this town from becoming the focus of new combat activities of the warring parties, to disable new militant groups from being brought in and deployed in the town that had been demilitarised earlier or in its vicinity. According to the assignment issued by the supreme command and the General Staff, the operational group needed to disarm paramilitary units and military detachments and prevent a town that had been peaceful and demilitarised for decades from being used for military purposes. It is important to emphasise that Dubrovnik had never, in a single plan, been marked as an objective, nor did anyone plan to occupy it. The only plan was to prevent the city from being used for military purposes. However, the Croatian political strategy was perfectly well aware of the strategic importance of Dubrovnik, and its "international importance" was used very skillfully for propaganda purposes. I will refer you to evidence that points to the fact that every initiative aimed at finding a peaceful solution for Dubrovnik was cut off. The Croatian authorities undermined every effort to demilitarise the town and establish normal communications in the area. Speaking of the composition of the 2nd Operational Group, it is also important to note that albeit it formally included corps, namely the 37th and the 2nd corps, as well as the military naval sector in the 2nd Operational Group, only parts of these corps and the military naval sector were actually engaged in the theatre of war. Operational levels of command in the corps and in the 9th VPS had forces engaged in combat activities at the same time as they kept other parts in the areas where these units were located in peacetime. Furthermore, it is important to emphasise that warfare and military skill in the former doctrine of the former JNA were divided into three levels: The strategic, operational, and tactical levels. According to that criterion, the commands of the land forces and the command of the naval district belonged to the strategic level of command as Witness Zorc pointed out as well. One step down was the operational level of command. The operational level of command included all corps commands, as well as military naval sectors. At the tactical level, there were commands of joint tactical units such as brigades, regiments, and battalions. A provisional, temporary formation such as the 2nd Operational Group can be categorised and must be categorised applying the principle of analogy; namely, if we take that the level of command is determined by the level of units and commands in question, we can see that the command of the 2nd Operational Group unified command over at least three operational commands and several commands of independent tactical units joined by a high degree of unity such as the 2nd Tactical Group and the 472nd Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Motorised Brigade. In other words, these three operative commands would be parts of the 37th Corps, 2nd Corps, and the 9th VPS. In keeping with these indisputable facts, the command of the 2nd Operational Group belongs to the strategic level, not the operational level which was at the end of the day confirmed by the Prosecution expert Milovan Zorc. It was important to emphasise this. Why is it important to establish to which level of command the 2nd Operational Group command belonged to? It is important because the commands of the operational and tactical levels have the duty to follow the chain of command and the conduct of their subordinate commanders and their units on a daily basis. This is particularly true of the units and commands in combat activities when front lines are fluid, borders are undefined, and there are similar circumstances. As opposed to these operational commands, the command on the strategic level, such as the 2nd Operational Group, is not only unable to follow from close quarters the functioning of the chain of decision-making and the conduct of subordinate commands; it is not even supposed to. Why? Because another level of command interfering in the daily functioning of command would certainly be too much. That is why the strategic level of command, such as the 2nd Operational Group, opts for the so-called "guiding, directing" role in issuing orders, and a totally different way of gaining insight into the conduct of units and individuals by carrying out team inspections of subordinates and interim reports and analysis. In our case, the case being tried here, we have one example that best illustrates this. It's Prosecution Exhibit P107 and Prosecution Exhibit P109. In order to gain an insight into how the system of command down the chain of command and lower down actually worked, the command at the strategic level, such the 2nd Operational Group, must rely on the official operational communications system alongside with its subordinate commands. Therefore, the 2nd Operational Group, as the strategic level of command, mostly bases its insights into the conduct and actions of its subordinates on intelligence gathered by its bodies, on data provided by its subordinates as part of their regular combat reports, and other aspects of operational communications such as briefings, reports, and the like. We shall see as we go through the evidence how these reports came from subordinate bodies, most of all from the 9th VPS to the 2nd Operational Group. It is entirely untrue that the commander of the 2nd OG was duty-bound to report on the conduct of battalion commanders, the forces that were in contact with enemy forces in the Dubrovnik area as has been suggested by some witnesses. The only thing the commander of the 2nd OG was able to do is use operational documents and combat reports sent to him by the commander of the 9th VPS down the chain of command and familiarise himself with the situation, to use the proposals of that commander to base his decisions on. Anything else he chose to do would not have been in compliance with the doctrine of command. It is obvious that it did indeed work that way, and we can see that clearly in the document where General Strugar requests proposals from his subordinate commanders as well as in other documents in which it is clear that his subordinates did, in fact, provide such proposals. Documents have been admitted that show precisely this sort of communication between the 2nd Operational Group and the 9th VPS and its commander. In relation to command and control in the 2nd Operational Group as a temporary formation, there were certain other peculiarities that were unusual for the doctrine of command in the JNA. Was it on account of the problematic and difficult circumstances that made the situation throughout the country very complex that they came about? There was a peculiar relationship between the 9th VPS and the military naval district, between the 9th VPS and the VPO. It ran counter to the established military doctrine which has been confirmed by Prosecution Witness Zorc; namely, the 9th VPS had been temporarily resubordinated to the 2nd Operational Group. However, between October and December 1991, it received and carried out orders from the command of the military naval district, such as order D105, Defence Exhibit 105. The commander of the 9th VPS, Jokic, pursuant to an order from the command of the military naval district ordered the lifting of the naval blockade of Dubrovnik, although at the time this ran counter to orders that he had received from the General Staff and orders he had received from the 2nd Operational Group. Besides, there are numerous other orders throughout the period relevant to this indictment that Jokic testified to. He particularly underlined the numerous tasks of the 9th VPS, arduous tasks carried out by the 9th VPS, in relation to the evacuation of units and garrisons of the military naval district and moving them to Boka; the entire manpower, equipment, weapons, materiel, under war circumstances or circumstances that were nearly war circumstances. Those orders, however, had never been issued to him by Strugar or by the 2nd Operational Group; they had been issued by the command of the military naval district, as Witness Jokic pointed out a number of times during his testimony and in the interviews that he provided to the OTP. You can also see that the information centre of the 9th VPS sent information on to the military naval district and the General Staff. They filed and submitted regular combat reports to the command of the 2nd Operational Group, but also to the military naval district. They sent information reports to the military naval district, intelligence reports. Daily logistics reports were forwarded to the 2nd Operational Group and the military naval district. Interim reports were submitted to the military naval district. The operations centre of the 9th VPS forwarded relevant information to the VPO, and information on activities and reconnaissance were obtained by the VPO from the 9th VPS. There are documents showing this that have been admitted. It is important to note this because dual responsibility and subordination were a hindrance to control and command within the 2nd Operational Group. In this context, there was a special problem because the commander of the 9th VPS failed to report to the command of the 2nd Operational Group on events of particular significance within his own area of responsibility. For example, in relation to informing his superior command about the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December 1991, Jokic stated as follows. He says that informing the commander of the 2nd Operational Group of that particular event for him would have constituted a pure waste of time. The transcript reference is 4.047. The commander of the 9th VPS did not inform the 2nd Operational Group about the attack on Srdj, about how the operation was carried out, or what the consequences were. No reports were ever sent, even just for notification or to the attention of a certain unit which other documents have shown, when, for example, the commander of the 9th VPS informs the federal secretariat for national defence or the naval district and sends a document on also to the 2nd Operational Group, or rather, to the attention of the 2nd Operational Group. Now, these -- for their information only. Now, these events on the 6th of December were crucial. Yet, the 9th VPS never informed the 2nd OG about them. We have also seen much evidence to the effect that the VPS had direct communication, that they sent reports and received orders from the General Staff and the federal secretariat for national defence, bypassing the 2nd Operational Group in the process. Witness Zorc assumes that the command of the 2nd Operational Group was in a much more unfavourable position in relation to the command of the VPO in terms of how stable the system of command and control was. He says this based on his personal acquaintance with command personnel of the 9th VPS, the 2nd OG, and also in terms of the degree of trust it had enjoyed among its subordinate units. Witness Zorc believes this affected how effectively the system of command and control worked in the 2nd OG, how effectively it could exercise command and control over the 9th VPS, which was subordinate to it. Parallel lines of command and dual command will always provoke this kind of problem. It must be pointed out that commanders of the 2nd Operational Group, having toured the units that were part of the 2nd Operational Group, did issue the relevant orders and instructions to remedy the weaknesses that had been noticed and to remove those weaknesses. P107 and P109 clearly show this. Also, in their decisions on further activities and operations, the 2nd Operational Group ordered the prevention and suppression of all undesirable occurrences. The commander of the 2nd Operational Group on several different occasions explicitly banned operations against Dubrovnik and the Old Town. Those were orders to subordinate units that were crystal clear. Furthermore, in contrast to that, it's important to point out another indisputable fact. If you look at the combat reports of the commander of the 9th VPS that he sent to the 2nd Operational Group and to other superior levels of command, as in the case of Admiral Brovet, the federal secretary for national defence or the chief of the General Staff, there was never any reference to units of the 9th VPS targeting the Old Town. Witness Jokic provided testimony here that was awkward, to say the least. He even went as far as to say that in the period between October and November 1991 he was not aware of that, but that in the course of his private investigation in 2002 and 2003, he was able to find out about that, and he decided to testify to that before this Honourable Trial Chamber; namely, that in October or November 1991, one of the units under his command had done that. For as long as he remained in his position as commander, there were never any reports to indicate damage to the Old Town. He never produced a single report indicating that while he was still commander. Furthermore, there is not a shred of evidence indicating that the commander of the 9th VPS requested a removal or made proposals for measures to be taken against anyone, any member of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, including, of course, the 3rd Battalion of the brigade. Likewise, in 2004, we heard testimony about alleged requests that were made for removal or dismissal. However, not a shred of hard evidence was given; only stories and people's accounts. Prosecution Witness Zorc found it necessary to agree with this. He studied this case, and he provided his findings. There is not a single written document making a request or proposal for anyone's removal with the addition of the report dated the 7th of December containing a reference to the removal of Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic who had arrived as stand-in for Commander Zdravkovic from the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade who was temporarily absent. Your Honours, I have now rounded off the first part of my closing argument. And now, I would like to pass the floor to my colleague, Mr. Petrovic, to cover some other areas. But maybe this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, Your Honours, by your leave, I would like to speak about something that the OTP referred to in their own final brief, and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that was referred to yesterday in the Prosecutor's closing argument, something that concerns discrepancies in the Defence theory in relation to what was said in the pre-trial brief and in the Defence's opening argument prior to the start of the Defence case. On two occasions, the Defence put forward our position and how we viewed the essence of our case. The first time was in October 2003, and the other time was on the 28th of June this year as part of the Defence's opening statement. I would like to briefly remind the Trial Chamber of what can be found in the pre-trial brief, the Defence pre-trial brief that was provided on the 1st of October 2003 where we pointed out a whole string of circumstances surrounding the creation and preparation of the pre-trial brief as well as how those circumstances affected the substance of our pre-trial brief. What I am speaking about and what is essential in that respect are paragraphs 4.7, point 8, point 9, and point 10 of the pre-trial brief dated the 1st of October 2003. One of these paragraphs, for example, says that the pre-trial brief cannot be considered as complete and entire because it does not include the necessary elements of analysis, such elements as it should include due to the way in which the pre-trial stage was conducted. In addition to which the Defence would like to point out that the pre-trial brief has been submitted without looking at the documents disclosed by the OTP, without going through key Defence witnesses' statements, and without studying the circumstances that OTP witnesses had invoked. Furthermore, on the 1st of October 2003, the Defence pointed out that it was highly likely that following the studying of the disclosed material, the Defence might take a different position, a position different to such allegations as were made in the pre-trial brief at the time. Also, when the time comes, the Defence would announce our position on the pre-trial brief. Therefore, for reasons that I will not go into now but that should be familiar by now, the pre-trial brief was just a mere indication of what the Defence case really was. And what was the Defence case? The Defence case is what this Trial Chamber has heard since the day our case was opened. That's what the Defence's case is. It is not in the least inconsistent, but rather it is perfectly clear what our submissions are, and we have furnished relevant and adequate proof for that. We believe those should be sufficient for the Trial Chamber to base their decision on. I would now like to go back to what the essence of our final brief will be. Above all, I'm about to focus on one of the units that was referred to many times and invoked many times throughout this trial; namely, the 472nd Motorised Brigade. This brigade was always part of the 9th VPS or part of the VPO. A lot of evidence has been produced to confirm that. Key aspects of the functioning of this unit were in all situations closely related to the military naval sector and district, regardless of the way in which this operational unit may have been used. I will use this opportunity to remind you of one aspect of the operational use of this unit, and this aspect has caused a certain amount of doubt during this trial. And this is an aspect that the OTP used through their key witness. It is the issue of promotion for members of the 472nd Motorised Brigade; more specifically, the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Regardless of the operational way in which this unit was used and the composition in which they carried out their combat activities, the procedures related to promotion, commendation and decoration were always linked to the 9th Military Naval Sector. So for example, Captain Kovacevic files a proposal to the command of the 9th VPS for promotion and incentives. The promotion and incentives proposed by Kovacevic include a commendation for the commander of the 9th VPS, the granting of special leave, and other incentives. All these incentives are supposed to be reward for combat activities carried out by the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade in November 1991. The chief of staff of the 9th VPS, Zec, Warship Captain Milan Zec, receives these proposals from Kovacevic, analyses the proposals, and forwards them to the assistant commander of the 9th VPS, Mihajlo Zarkovic for further consideration. D100 shows this very clearly, and this has been confirmed by what Defence witnesses testified to before this Trial Chamber. In his testimony before this Trial Chamber, the former commander of the naval military sector of Boka, Jokic, in as far as concerned promotion for members of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, he never missed a single opportunity to point out that General Strugar was the one who was in charge of those promotions and incentives and who awarded decorations and promotions. Documents that had been admitted as part of this trial, however, are in clear contradiction to that. D100 clearly shows how promotions were awarded in the 9th VPS and what sort of incentives were provided. Chief of Jokic's staff forwarded, for final decision-making, a list of members of the 3rd Battalion counting several dozens of names. He did so on the 6th of November 1991. Jokic was then not horrified by the fact that 100 members of that hateful brigade were being promoted. Only later when he found himself in prison does he begin to feel aghast at the fact that 100 of these members were commended, rewarded, and promoted. Jokic later describes the message that he sent to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade only ten days before the 6th of December when his command was doing all in their power to stimulate and commend members of that battalion for the results achieved so far. Only later when he found himself in prison does Jokic begin to distance himself from the members of this brigade, does he start telling stories about how he tried to expel them and replace them. But then, at the time, in 1994 -- sorry, in 1991, he was promoting them. Nowadays, however, he is ascribing all his deeds to Strugar. Strugar in his words was the one who was commending and promoting them, and the only thing that he can offer is his own story to corroborate this. As opposed to that, we have written documents and eyewitnesses speaking to the contrary. The 472nd Motorised Brigade did experience problems in its functioning. These problems that aggravated the functioning of this unit at the time, in autumn 1991, were shared by the entire Yugoslav People's Army and the entire Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There were problems in reinforcing units by mobilisation. The unit had to be reinforced by personnel from Dubrovnik, from the area of Dubrovnik. In view of the large number of reserve personnel from the area of Dubrovnik used to reinforce the unit, the unit was initially staffed largely short of establishment. There were many other problems in the functioning of that brigade because of the shortage of adequate military-recorded specialties. Those who were properly trained for certain activities had not responded to the call-up. And it was, therefore, impossible to reinforce and staff the units properly. Additional personnel had to be found from other areas, including young soldiers who were only in the process of training and without having completed the training had to be engaged in view of the situation as we've heard many times here. Also, in the period of September and October 1991, this unit was reinforced by a large number of officers who had never before been members of that unit. In end September, only 40 per cent of active-duty officers, or rather the unit had only 40 per cent of the establishment in terms of active-duty officers. The officers that were engaged came from the reserve officers school in Bileca who were attached to the unit on a temporary basis. And as we know from the evidence before this Trial Chamber, these officers enjoyed respect among the troops. Although these facts are not to be neglected, the witnesses we heard testified that despite all the problems, these officers managed to bring discipline up to an adequate level. Those were witnesses Lemal, Stojanovic and others whose testimony is especially noteworthy and valuable because their units were directly engaged in the blockade of Dubrovnik, and therefore of special interest to us. Another fact that should not be neglected is very important because it has been mentioned before this Trial Chamber so frequently. The command climate. Only several days before the beginning of combat operations, Commander Nojko Marinovic deserted his unit, and not only that, he goes on to become the commander of the units that the 472nd Motorised Brigade had to meet in combat. That fact was particularly defeating for the members of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, the fact that their commander became the commander of the opposing side with all the knowledge that he possessed about the deployment, combat disposition, and strength of their forces. Speaking of the command climate, the Prosecution witness Pringle spoke at length about it, but he spoke about what he knew and what his experience was from the British Army and other armies. I don't believe that he had ever, in considering command climate of a unit, to imagine the effect the desertion of a commander can have on a unit and the later becoming by that commander of -- and the later assumption by that commander of commanding position over the warring party's unit. I don't think that he had ever had such experience in another foreign army. That, however, is precisely the situation that Pavle Strugar had to face. But generally speaking, it was a totally abnormal situation overall, when the whole state was in the process of disappearing, together with its army, to be replaced by five different armies. That is the situation in which Pavle Strugar was supposed to create an appropriate command climate in which to execute the tasks given him by the superior command. In addition to that, Witness Pringle, when cross-examined, confirmed that he had not even studied the regulations prevailing in the former JNA; that is, the armed forces of the SFRY. He said instead that his observations about the way in which a new commander should create a command climate in a new unit were based on his experience in the British Army, which makes his allegations made here completely pointless and deprived of sense. Coming back to the issue of the 472nd Brigade, I should like to add that the commander of the 9th VPS stipulated in his orders not only the execution of combat activities, but also other aspects that affected the life and operation of the units of this brigade or the landing and assault brigade or whatever else we called it before this Trial Chamber. That includes the establishment of the communications network and system, and in this context I should like to refer to a document which is in evidence. It shows that the command of the 9th VPS stipulates in its decisions also the composition and the equipment of units within the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Everybody in this courtroom will certainly remember how many times Admiral Jokic sitting in the witness box cried how much he had done to remove heavy artillery away from Dubrovnik, to replace the 3rd Battalion because its equipment was too heavy, all because of his concerns, his overwhelming concerns for the Old Town of Dubrovnik. But he's saying all this in year 2004, Your Honours. Leaving the 9th VPS, the 472nd Brigade is asking to be given back the battery of ZIS cannons that had been detached and became a separate unit within the composition of the 9th VPS. The command of the brigade leaving the 9th VPS asked back the ZIS cannons that were -- that had been given to the 3rd Battalion because they were under Kovacevic's command outside Dubrovnik. They're asking for them because they needed them for Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond combat activities elsewhere within their zone of responsibility. However, although the brigade asked for this in writing from Jokic, what does Jokic answer? He says: "Look into possibilities." And that's all. In year 2004, Jokic testifies before you, Your Honours, and he says that he had invested superhuman efforts to remove the artillery, being aware of the possibility of hitting of the Old Town. And again, he blames Strugar for the failure to remove the artillery. Those, Your Honours, are only empty words of Miodrag Jokic, a man who is desperate to minimise his criminal liability and to satisfy the expectations of the Office of the Prosecutor. What Jokic actually said was "look into possibilities." However, his chief of staff Milan Zec was much more specific. Zec ordered ZIS cannons then on the 23rd of November 1991 that they cannot be removed from the 3rd Battalion. Why? Because they had to stay there until the problem of Mount Srdj is solved because two weeks prior to the 6th December, Zec would not give away the cannons until the problem is solved. I refer you to the document where all this is written. It is D106. He recognised his own handwriting there as well as the handwriting of the then-Warship Commander Captain Zec. However, the only thing that he fails to remember in 2004 was the contents of that document; namely, the problem of Mount Srdj. In 1991, as we can see from this document, Jokic and his command were facing the problem of Srdj. Nowadays, in 2004, Jokic's problem seems to be the Old Town. Then, like now, Jokic is not hesitant, neither in 1991 when he was solving the problem of Srdj, nor today when Jokic was faced with a problem of blaming and shifting all the responsibility, all the criminal liability to General Strugar. In 1991, that battalion, as we heard many times, was part of the 472nd Brigade up until the 20th November 1991 when the brigade subordinated to the 2nd Corps -- when the brigade was subordinated to the 2nd Corps, whereas the 3rd Battalion remained under the command of the 9th VPS. What does matter and what the Defence should like the Trial Chamber to consider especially carefully is the combat engagement of the 3rd Battalion. The theory of our Defence is that on the 6th of December, there was no possibility whatsoever to consider that, on the basis of what happened in October and November, there was a substantial risk regarding the way the unit was used on the positions involved in the immediate blockade of the town of Dubrovnik. Why am I saying this, Your Honours? In October, that battalion did not take part in any combat operations in the immediate vicinity of Dubrovnik. It didn't take part in November either. More precisely, it didn't take part in any way that could create the fear that it could be deployed on the said positions. And I will clarify this now. In November 1991, as we know, Bosanka, Kula, and Strincijera were taken. And the 3rd Battalion remains there up until the beginning of 1992; that is, the time relevant for our indictment. From the 20th November onwards, the battalion was detached from the brigade and subordinated directly to the command of the 9th VPS to block the town from the south and southeast side. I will remind you that Witness Lemal stated before this Court that in October, this unit had not taken part in combat operations. Witness A, as we know, is one of company commanders. Another company commander in that battalion also confirms that beginning with mid-October, the 3rd Battalion had been withdrawn, pulled back, and given leave in the area of Talezi village. There was the commander of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion. Captain Stojanovic speaks of the fact that beginning with the 1st October 1991 in operations in which ten men from his unit had been killed, confirms that the unit had been withdrawn and given leave in the Talez village already in mid-October. These are facts that were mentioned here several times referring to the events of the 23rd, 24th, 25th October, whichever date is correct. The 3rd Battalion, however, does not take part in these operations. It is on leave in the area of Talez village, which is clear from the testimony of Witnesses Lemal and Stojanovic, and it is also clear from the documents in evidence relating to this period. In combat to the east of Dubrovnik in October, the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Brigade did take place. On a map, P120, you can clearly see how the positions of the 4th Battalion were moved from positions at Celopeci, Bujici village towards Donji Brgat, Gornji Brgat, and so on. If you look at that document, the fact comes across with great clarity. In November, starting with the 10th of November, pursuant to a direct order from Jokic, the 3rd Battalion was involved in combat. However, the manner of their involvement was particularly significant, what the role of the 3rd Battalion was in events which started on 10th of November 1991. If you look at all the orders that we have in evidence in relation to the events on the 10th, 11th, and 12th, and the operations that were to follow in those days, this battalion was used only as an infantry unit, and their task was to seize a certain axis, including Mount Srdj. The issue of artillery, the issue of mortars, the issue of potential sources of fire allegedly damaging the Old Town in November 1991 has nothing whatsoever to do with the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. The brigade was then used merely as an infantry unit to take a line. Of course, they were enjoying fire support; however, it is clear, and I will confirm this, that this fire support was provided by other units from the 9th VPS and not this one. Not at any point in time was there infantry attacks supported by any of the integral parts of the 3rd Battalion. The attack was supported by units from outside the 3rd Battalion, units under the 9th VPS pursuant to clear and detailed instructions from Jokic about the use of artillery support during the 3rd Battalion's attack on the 10th, 11th, and 12th against such lines as were designated, and this is confirmed by the evidence before this Trial Chamber. The Defence would also like to point out that there is a great deal of discrepancy between combat orders of the commander of the 9th VPS for the 10 -- for the 9th and the 10th of November respectively. In relation to the attack on the 9th of November, there are no orders specifying the use of mortars and artillery. However, if you look at the regular combat report of the 9th VPS on the 10th of November, you can see that units of the 9th VPS involved in fighting on that day could not break through to the lines that the commander of the 9th VPS had ordered them to reach, including reaching Srdj. In his next combat order, he orders the use of artillery and mortars on the 11th of November to provide support for his units carrying out the attack. The focus of artillery fire as ordered by Jokic was in the area of Srdj, Strincijera, Gradac and Dubrave. Further, the next day, the 12th of November 1991, Jokic orders the stepping up of artillery and mortar fire. In none of those situations did the artillery or the mortars whose activity was being requested were the mortars or the artillery that were actually attached to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. For the 473rd Battalion was the battalion that was used for infantry operations, for support, and was the potential source of damage to the Old Town. And they draw on the sector units beginning with the TOC, the 1070 AG, the Howitzer battery, 120-millimetre Howitzers, and so on and so forth. I will not go any further into this, Your Honours. This is all in D57, D58, and D126, in one word, documents that were written and produced by Jokic stipulating how units of the 9th VPS should be used on the 10th, 11th, and 12th of November 1991. If we look at the three combat orders that I have referred to, the commander of the 9th VPS clearly orders the taking of Srdj. He orders his troops to reach the Srdj elevation. It comes across with great clarity on the basis of these documents. This is no matter of interpretation. There are no different interpretations. And it's not about how Jokic remembers this to be 13 years since. It is clearly shown by these documents. Today Jokic claims that, for example, if you take the Srdj-Strincijera line it doesn't necessarily mean that you need to take Srdj, but rather that you need to take an area which is at a distance of about several hundred metres from Srdj itself. But that's where the original position is from which these units are starting out because that's where the village of Bosanka is, several hundred metres away from Srdj, several hundred metres away from Srdj, about 700 metres away from Srdj, you have the fort of Strincijera itself. All these distances between the topographical points on this map are as a rule several hundred metres. Therefore, the mortars and artillery that were used on the 10th, 11th, and 12th of November were the mortars and the artillery from the 9th VPS, but not from the composition of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. If indeed there was any damage that was caused to the Old Town in November, then it was caused by Jokic's own artillery. It is clear based on his orders what the role of the 3rd Battalion was, and it is quite obvious what the role of the artillery units was. And again, we have a discrepancy between what Jokic claims and what the documents tell us. Jokic would have us believe that what he wrote and ordered back in 1991 is not true. He would have us believe what he's telling us now in 2004. He would like to have us believe what he's telling us in 2004 as he awaits the outcome of his appeal to a sentence that was imposed on him and as he awaits a decision by the OTP on the exact degree of his cooperation and as he awaits a ruling from the Trial Chamber pursuant to his appeal in which he claims that the exact degree of cooperation with the OTP was not sufficiently appreciated during the trial of General Strugar. At this point in time, it might be interesting to go through some allegations made by the OTP in connection with Jokic related to a number of different factors that might affect his sentence. These factors go to the very essence of Jokic's testimony nevertheless. You remember how yesterday the OTP, in a very moving way I must say, portrayed Jokic as a moderate man, a measured man who has no reason on earth to tell anything but the truth. They portrayed him as a peace-loving person who is only here for the sake of the truth. However, the OTP choose to overlook the following facts, that this same person had concluded an agreement with the OTP that also stipulates what sort of sentence would be handed out in return for which he is supposed to cooperate, to give interviews whenever required to do so. Following his testimony, the OTP provides an assessment of his testimony which in turn affects the length of his sentence. And this assessment might be that he failed to cooperate or that he cooperated insufficiently. The assessment could have been that he cooperated fully in the Strugar trial. Jokic waged his own war in his testimony. He struggled for his own sake. The Trial Chamber should know that, and the OTP knows that very well. He struggled to reduce his own sentence. Besides, General Strugar, due to his own poor health, is not able to take the stand himself and testify to refute what Jokic said. All of the documents that were used in this case were disclosed to Jokic, so Jokic is in possession of all this information. Jokic also knows that all the elements that the OTP bases the responsibility of General Strugar on were actually extracted from Jokic's own testimony. All the allegations that are not in relation to the crime base stem from Jokic's testimony. It is Jokic that is the OTP case because if you take Jokic away from their case, they have nothing. And yesterday, they chose to call him "disinterested." He's not a disinterested party because he is awaiting a decision in a trial where he was one of the original indictees. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Therefore, the claim made yesterday by the OTP is simply incredible. Also, after Jokic's testimony on the 9th of August 2004, the OTP accepted that the Chamber allegedly made a mistake in relation to certain facts regarding Admiral Jokic and that his sentence was to be modified accordingly. What I find significant is the time frame in which all of this is happening. Had Jokic had a choice, had he been in a position to choose, could he have testified differently, knowing that there was an appeal underway and that the outcome of this appeal to a very high degree hinged on the assessment of the OTP, the very same OTP pressing charges against General Strugar. The OTP and Jokic are on the same case in a manner of speaking. They're pursuing the same goal in this case. Only their reasons are different. The OTP wishes to win a case based on nothing. All the documents that are in evidence clearly show that Witness Jokic's testimony is completely untruthful in reference to Srdj, in reference to Jokic's testimony before this Trial Chamber where allegedly all his efforts were directed at removing the artillery and the mortars from the vicinity of the Old Town, saying that he never authorised fire on Srdj because he was aware, he claims, that every time Srdj was missed, the Old Town would have been hit. He also claims that he never ordered the taking of the fortress at Srdj. Admiral Jokic's allegations today are in open and obvious contradiction to his written orders produced at the time as well as other authentic documents that have been tendered throughout this trial. They merely represent an attempt to justify his own role in these events and to dodge responsibility. As far as the evidence before this Trial Chamber is concerned, there is not a single document that would link General Pavle Strugar and the 2nd OG to anything going on round Srdj, stepping up the blockade of Dubrovnik, or the activity of mortars around Dubrovnik. There is nothing to indicate that he ordered fire to be opened on Srdj or that he planned to have the fortress and the feature at Srdj taken. On the 13th of November 1991 a cease-fire came into effect. A truce between the Croatian forces and the JNA forces along the line of the town of Dubrovnik. Negotiations continued between the Croatian forces and the JNA, with the mediation of Minister Bernard Kouchner. The objective was to have a permanent cease-fire and for life for Dubrovnik to go back to normal. Between the 13th of November and the 6th of December, there were numerous acts of provocation by firing carried out by the Croatian forces against JNA forces in the area around Dubrovnik. There are documents showing that, and this issue has been addressed fully in our final brief. I am not going into details now since details can be found in these documents and in our brief. The only thing I would like to say now in connection with the 3rd Battalion, without going into what happened on the 6th of December and the full impact of what happened, I would like to say something about the use of mortars by that battalion on the 6th of December 1991 from the perspective of what Jokic stated in one of his interviews. Witness Jokic stated that once he had been informed on the 6th of December that the 3rd Battalion was under fire by the Croatian side, he decided the battalion had its own artillery and that their artillery should be used to neutralise the fire that was putting them at risk. That's what Jokic stated in an interview to the OTP in July 2002 on page 204 of that interview. When asked by the Defence whether Kovacevic had received instructions to use his own artillery if no support had been forthcoming, Jokic answered, "Of course." Further, Witness Jokic also stated in the interview: "I told him that he had his own artillery, I mean Kovacevic, and that he should neutralise those firing positions," and the reference is to the firing positions of the Croatian side. Jokic stated that to the OTP in July 2002 on page 205. Having no choice, he confirmed these words when asked by the Defence before this Honourable Trial Chamber. Therefore, it was Admiral Jokic who ordered that the artillery of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade be used to neutralise the firing positions. Before he set out for Belgrade, Jokic had sent a message to Zec that he should complete the withdrawal, that he should prevent any further losses to the battalion and that he should neutralise any danger to the battalion. That is what Witness Jokic stated to the OTP in July 2002 on page 207, and he confirmed these allegations before the Trial Chamber. Therefore, we submit that on the 6th of December, the Old Town of Dubrovnik could have been targeted from two possible sources, the artillery of the 9th VPS or the mortars of the 3rd Battalion. Admiral Jokic personally ordered that any fire coming from the town of Dubrovnik, and he mentioned nothing about the Old Town itself, should be neutralised by the artillery of the 3rd Battalion. Therefore, the Defence concludes unequivocally that all the alleged damage that could have been incurred to the Old Town of Dubrovnik or Dubrovnik as a whole could have been caused only by the use of artillery and mortars. And in any situation, no matter what the situation is, be it the sector artillery or the mortars of the 3rd Battalion, their use was authorised by Miodrag Jokic. By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to turn briefly to the problem on the opposing side, the Croatian side; namely, the militarisation of the town of Dubrovnik, the town which in the times of the SFRY was freed from all the garrisons that were moved to the hinterland in order to enable the development of tourism. I will remind you of a witness who said that the demilitarisation of Dubrovnik was one of the prerequisites for the town's acquisition of the UNESCO protection and the World Heritage status. In our submissions from July and August, we noted that members of the ZNG, the National Guard Corps, had occupied back in July, according to the establishment scheme, the town of Dubrovnik. Prosecution Exhibit 116, including a map indicating the strength of forces occupying the town of Dubrovnik. The 116th Brigade consisted of two battalions; seven battalions had 12 offices, 11 commanding offices.
