utterances.text: [Interpretation] In total, the Croatian forces had 1.146 members, including 80 officers and NCOs. In the events surrounding Dubrovnik, what mattered a lot to the Croatian propaganda effort was Dubrovnik in its attempts to effect secession from the SFRY. We have documents in evidence to show that in certain periods Croatian forces were deployed in Bogosica Park. Witness Negodic, looking at photographs from that period, recognised Zoran Primic opening fire from a mortar dressed in civilian clothing. Witness Negodic incorrectly interprets the activity of this mortar. But that is elaborated in our final brief. On P160, mortar positions of the Croatian forces are marked east of the gate to the Old Town as well as the anti-aircraft weapon on the northern wall on the Old Town. On map P159, we see the position of the mortar in the vicinity of the eastern gate to the Old Town. From the same position in the immediate vicinity of the eastern gate to the Old Town, there are indications of the axes and directions of fires towards Bosanka, Brgat, and Zarkovica. Witness Negodic also stated that he didn't have enough sighting devices for the artillery used which caused disbelief, disbelief that such weapons could have been used at all. We heard that from Colonel Poje. The Croatian forces also had vehicle-mounted mortars which moved quickly and silently. They would fire and rapidly disappear. We had a number of witnesses who testified about this. They changed the positions from which they fired so quickly that even an experienced journalist like Davis, journalist Davis, could not observe them. Witnesses described firing positions near Belvedere and Argentina Hotels. Witness Davis mentioned firing from the vicinity of the Argentina Hotel. The target was the JNA unit on the hill above them. Witness Davis also testified that he had noticed an anti-aircraft gun mounted on top of a truck frequently changing position. He saw it in the new harbour of Dubrovnik near the police station, although other witnesses testified that they had seen it in other places in Dubrovnik. The tactic of the Croatian forces was to fire and move away immediately. The Croatian side did this in order to avoid returned fire by the JNA. Quick shots and rapid changes of position that were so quick that Davis did not manage to film them could lead us to the incorrect conclusion that the returned fire directed at the Croatian mortar actually targeted a civilian position because when the returned fire would arrive, the Croatian mortar had already moved to a different firing position. Thus, we could be led to believe that the JNA units had acted without provocation, which was not the case as we can see clearly from the evidence. In the video footage given this Court by Witness Grbic, we see artillery weapons in Gradac. Gradac is in the immediate vicinity of the Old Town. It is right next to the Lovrinac fort which is part of the cultural heritage of Dubrovnik. We see fire being opened from a mortar in Bogosica Park. What is especially noteworthy in this video which we called Grbic's video, that is P66, we see a member of the Croatian forces, part of the crew of a three-barrel gun, and a witness says, describing these events, "on the 6th of December, it seemed like we had five or six such guns precisely because we changed locations so rapidly. The mortar would look for us and damage the town, but they couldn't find us." And that confirms the statements made by Defence witnesses who said that the Croatian forces opened fire, moved quickly, and thus provoked return fire by the JNA. Very briefly, I would now like to turn to firing activity from the Old Town because I believe we made our submissions in detail in our final brief. Witness Nesic, Witness Drljan, and Witness Pepic spoke about this. What is especially interesting as the Trial Chamber certainly knows is the number of targets in the Old Town marked by Witness Nesic. However, what I would like to say at this moment regarding Witness Nesic, and you will find the details in evidence, of course, I would like to emphasise that all that Witness Nesic observed in 1991 he described to members of the OTP in 2003 in the interview he gave them in Belgrade. That interview was led by the trial team leader in this case. Obviously satisfied with what they heard from Nesic in that interview, they put Jovica Nesic on the Prosecution's list of witnesses as a Prosecution witness in this case. Jovica Nesic's testimony as the Trial Chamber certainly knows was expected and planned by the Prosecution. Through the state authorities of Serbia and Montenegro, the Prosecution made considerable efforts to force Nesic to testify. They summoned him, and only when he refused to testify as a Prosecution witness did they remove him from the Prosecution's witness list, and the Trial Chamber was informed of this, if I'm not mistaken, in March or April this year. All that Nesic told the Prosecution in November 2003 and based on which the Prosecution had been looking forward for so long to his testimony, we did not hear. Nowadays, they say that they regret the fact he didn't testify. We know today that there are significant discrepancies in what he said in 2003 about the activity of Croatian forces. Speaking to the investigators in 2003 in Belgrade, Nesic even drew a layout of the Croatian forces in 1991. And as we know, that little map, that sketch, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond was disclosed to us only last year. You will find all the relevant facts in our final brief. I would only like to take up something that was said yesterday about what can and cannot be seen from Zarkovica. We heard a lot about whether the Old Town can be seen from Zarkovica, whether a human silhouette can be made out, whether a mortar can be noticed, seen, with the naked eye or with binoculars. Witnesses were shown video footage with the worst possible definition in order to challenge statements that mortars can be indeed seen from Zarkovica, and the Prosecutor referred to superhuman sight. However, the Defence had resolved this dilemma long ago. The Prosecutor also tried to challenge the evidence of Pepic and Drljan that they had seen what they had seen because allegedly they couldn't have seen it because of the great distance. However, Pepic said that he not only had military binoculars, but at Zarkovica, he had a special periscope which as required could be used for observing targets in the town of Dubrovnik and its immediate vicinity. As regards negotiations that were conducted constantly with the Croatian side, this has been clarified in detail in our final brief. I would only like to say a few words about the so-called 11-point proposal. That proposal was made by the 2nd Operative Group in concurrence with the staff of the superior command and the proposal refers to the surrender of artillery weapons and other weapons, demilitarisation, and it constitutes an attempt to resolve all the problems that stand in the way of restoring the supply of electricity and other necessities to the town. However, we heard yesterday and we read in the Prosecutor's final brief that in their understanding, this document is actually a mimicry by General Strugar to conceal his "real nature," as the Prosecutor puts it, the real nature of a man who only wants war and destruction. However, the Prosecution overlooks certain facts. That is a document not made by General Strugar. That document was drafted with the closest cooperation of the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY. This also begs the question, was Bernard Kouchner also a warmonger? The key propositions of that agreement that was signed between the JNA and the representatives of Dubrovnik on the 5th of December with the support and at the initiative even of Bernard Kouchner include identical items as the 11-point proposal, points referring to the withdrawal of forces, disarming of Croatian forces, and departure of all military elements coming from outside. The 11-point proposal in many ways reflects the agreement that had been reached earlier between the JNA and the citizens of Dubrovnik with the support of Kouchner that had been, however, blocked by the Croatian authorities. The Prosecution tries to portray General Strugar as a man who can never get enough of war as opposed to what he really is, a general who is trying to achieve peace, whose forces are under attack. Jokic was a different man, according to the Prosecutor. His only concern was to negotiate peace. This is a totally artificial creation of the Prosecutor. The conduct of Jokic in the zone of Dubrovnik was not led by his own propensities and inclinations. Combat operations were conducted only when the supreme command ordered them. Jokic did not participate in negotiations with ambassadors in October or Minister Rudolf in November, December, because he loved peace. He went to those negotiations because he was ordered by telegram by the General Staff, as we can see from the record. He went to the negotiations in December under orders given him by General Kandic. Very briefly, perhaps for just one minute, I would like to speak about the implementation of the December negotiations and the way in which Jokic was engaged in these negotiations. He said -- in fact, I would say that Jokic's claim that such a high representative of the 9th naval sector was in that situation a mere messenger because as Jokic puts it, coming from Belgrade to Podgorica, he was passing through Vis and Kumbor, and since he was in Kumbor, Strugar asked him to pass on the information from the meeting in Belgrade. I would call that claim absolutely incorrect. It is unimaginable that messages would be passed in this way to the commander on such -- in such a high position, in such a complex situation with the presence of all the complex and sophisticated communications systems. It is also unimaginable that Pavle Strugar if indeed he had been given orders in Belgrade to forward orders to Commander Jokic, that Strugar would do so in passing through Kumbor. In addition to that, we have to bear in mind the fact that on the 5th of December 1991, Jokic was negotiating on behalf of the supreme command of the armed forces. On the 7th of December in that capacity, he signed the agreement. In neither of these situations did he act as commander of the 2nd Operational Group or the 9th VPS. From the available evidence, the Defence draws the conclusion that at the meeting of the General Staff, it was decided that Jokic should represent the armed forces and through the uninterrupted channels of communications Jokic was so informed. I believe, Your Honour, this is a convenient moment for the lunch break. With your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We will now adjourn, resuming at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In this part of our closing argument, the Defence will try as briefly as possible to put to the Trial Chamber facts in connection with the 4th, 5th, and 6th of December 1991 which we addressed in some detail in our brief. Therefore, our summary now will be as brief as possible. As early as the 4th of December, there is a reference in the war log of the 9th VPS in Kupari, the Defence Exhibit Number is D96, and we see that the 9th VPS was informed that on that day, three ministers of the Croatian government and five envoys of the European Commission would be leaving Split and sailing to Dubrovnik. Furthermore, it was ascertained that the Croatian ministers came to their negotiations with the JNA on the 5th of December sailing on the Argosy ship, and they left Split at 8.15 in the morning. They arrived in Cavtat at 8.15 in the morning. The negotiations lasted until just after 12.00 on the 5th of December. And if we look at P162, which is the logbook of the Port Authority, the local port authority, you can see that the ship carrying the Croatian ministers and the members of the mission reached the Old Town harbour in Dubrovnik at 1248 hours. At these negotiations on the 5th of December, it was agreed that the negotiations should continue on the 6th, and that a cease-fire agreement should be signed. What remained unresolved on the 5th, which we heard in Minister's Rudolf's testimony as well as Jokic's testimony was the issue of how the ships sailing into Dubrovnik should be checked on the way. Admiral Jokic stated a reason that the agreement was not signed on the 5th. He said the reason was that he demanded ships be checked at open sea before they reached port, while the Croatian representatives demanded this be done as soon as they reached port at Gruz. Admiral Jokic, according to his testimony, told Minister Rudolf that he had to confer with the supreme command on this contentious issue. If we look at the regular combat report of the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector dated the 5th of December which was produced at 1700 hours at the Kupari forward command post, the commander of the 2nd Operational Group was sent there, and we see that the command of the 9th VPS never informed their superior command about an event as momentous as the negotiations that were afoot in Cavtat, negotiations which the commander of the 9th VPS took part himself. Neither does the combat report contain a single reference to anything that went on during those negotiations or to the cease-fire agreement and the start of a complete cease-fire that was supposed to take place on the 6th of December 1991 at 1200 hours. The Defence team wishes to draw particular attention to that part of Minister Rudolf's testimony, the part namely where Jokic tells him that he has to confer with the supreme command. This was is entirely in constanance [as interpreted] with the fact that it was precisely the supreme command of the armed force that had conferred upon him the authority to negotiate on their behalf with the highest representatives of the Croatian government and sign the agreement on their behalf eventually. This would seem to imply that Jokic was not truthful when he said that he had to confer with General Strugar regarding the checking of the ships. General Strugar never took part in those negotiations. He was never consulted, nor was he instructed on anything to do with those negotiations. There would have been no reason on earth to confer with Strugar on one issue only; namely, how the ships were to be checked. This would have been an issue outside his purview anyway. In addition to this, the Defence team wishes to point out that this issue of checking the ships throughout all the rounds of negotiations that had been conducted had never been posed or presented as a problem before, nor had it been included in the 11 points that were proposed by the OG in order to help life in Dubrovnik to go back to normal. The Defence team believes that Jokic's statement about negotiations between the highest possible Croatian government level and the armed forces of the SFRY pursuant to the agreement that had previously been signed in Geneva on the 23rd of November by President Tudjman, Croatian President Tudjman, and the general secretary for national defence, Kadijevic, and facing a situation where there had already been many casualties as a result of the hostilities, Jokic proposed that an agreement be signed just because, as he said, he was concerned about the safety of one or two of his officers who were supposed to be part of the team checking the ships. He raises the issue of the safety of JNA officers in the Gruz harbour, but this cannot be viewed as the key issue or the key issue that stopped the agreement from being signed. That agreement envisaged a total cease-fire and the setting up of mixed commissions as well as other measures to be adopted in order to restore the trust between the warring parties, all under the auspices of the European Community. We would also like to point out the supreme command of the armed forces in connection with these negotiations had given up some of their most crucial demands, demands that had been made in relation to Dubrovnik previously; above all, those concerning weapons, those concerning armed units leaving Dubrovnik. Therefore, the only reason that the agreement was actually not signed on the 5th of December was Jokic's desire to resolve the search problem prior to the signing of the agreement. And here is why: On the very same day, the 5th of December, in the morning hours at 915 hours, an order arrived from the General Staff at the forward command post in Kupari, an order issued by the chief, Blagoje Adzic himself, saying that an African ship called Cape Africa should be allowed to sail into the Dubrovnik harbour on the 5th of December. As the negotiations between Rudolf and Jokic were concluded just past 1200 hours on the 5th, the logbook of the 9th VPS shows an entry at 1330 hours the same day, after the negotiations were concluded. The entry shows Jokic ordering that the ship Cape Africa not be allowed into Dubrovnik before the 6th of December, thus directly opposing an order which had arrived from the chief of the General Staff. It is very typical that Jokic should in this way refuse to carry out an order that had been received from the chief of the General Staff. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond This decision was adopted immediately after the conclusion of the negotiations in Cavtat. There are other facts that provide indications about his preparations for the 6th of December. If you look at the war log at 855 hours in the morning of the 5th of December, the head of the European Mission to Dubrovnik sent a message to the VPS in Boka requesting authorisation for himself and a team of experts to use the regular boat line running between Dubrovnik and Mokosica on the 6th of December. It was a local, regular boat line that had already been restored by then, to be allowed to come to Komolac to inspect and carry out reparations on a water station that was there. This had been discussed earlier. This request was received at Kupari. Again, on the 5th of December at 1105 hours, Boka received a request from the commissioner for the Red Cross in Dubrovnik, Stanko Kozeli, who asked to be granted safe passage on the Argosy ship to Cavtat and back on the 6th of December in order to transport humanitarian assistance that was supposed to be taken over by the Herceg Novi Red Cross. Also on the same day, the 5th of December at 1715 hours, the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff sends a request to the Boka VPS in reference to the agreement that had been achieved earlier in the day by the representatives of the Croatian government and proposes that the ship called Arka should leave the Gruz harbour the next day carrying humanitarian aid to the island of Sipan. So all these are local traffic lines, and all these were to be used for the Red Cross to travel. What exactly is going on here? In the coastal radio log in reference to the 5th of December, the Dubrovnik Port Authority, P162, as early as 1905 hours, a answer from the VPS in Boka was received. The reply stated that these requests for these three ships to sail on the 6th of December could not be met, nor could the safety of the ships and persons be guaranteed. It was underlined that the VPS command was prepared to deal on these issues very soon, which would above all depend on the outcome of the negotiations in Cavtat on the 6th of December. If we go back to the talks and the contentious issue there, the problem seemed to be ships coming from outside Dubrovnik and not the local lines. Also, if we go back to the message by the Boka VPS, the message they sent to Dubrovnik, the logbook at Kupari reflects it as being made at 2012 hours. That means 11 hours after the people in Dubrovnik had received the message. This begs the following question: Why in contradiction to the agreement that had been reached on the 5th are these local lines banned in relation to the 6th? Why should the Cape Africa ship not be allowed to enter Dubrovnik when this had been approved by the chief of the General Staff? What is the reasoning behind this decision by the VPS? Perhaps they needed to resolve the search problem first of all. That certainly is the position of the Defence team. There is another thing that must be taken into account. If Dubrovnik had received the message at 1905 hours and it was received and recorded in Kupari at 2020 hours, that means the message must have come from the basic command post at Kumbor. Who was there at the time? The commander of the 9th VPS, Jokic. Some of the Defence witnesses commented at length on the briefings that were held at Kupari, when the briefings took place, who chaired the briefings, and who was present. The briefings were used by units to inform their superior command about what was going on after which interim combat reports -- regular combat reports were produced and sent on to the superior command. On the 5th of December, Witness Jovanovic attended a briefing at the Kupari forward command post, which he testified to in detail. The briefing was attended by the commanders of subordinate units, the commander of the 9th VPS, the chief of staff of the 9th VPS, as well as Captain Kovacevic. Witness Jovanovic spoke at length before this Chamber about the substance of that meeting and about the plan according to which everything unfolded, how the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December was planned and approved. Witness Jovanovic, on the 6th of December, after his unit had engaged in combat operations, after he had previously informed orally on the activities of his unit drew up a written report on the 6th of December at 1400 hours, and this was delivered to the command of the 9th VPS. From this report, we can see under item 2 that on the previous day, the 5th of December, he was present when Kovacevic outlined in detail the plans for the operations of the 6th of December, that the commander of the 9th VPS was present at the time, and that Chief of Staff Zec intervened to have combat activities completed by 1200 hours on the 6th of December. This is all contained in a document drawn up in 1991. On the 23rd of July 2004, Witness Jokic said that there had been no briefing at the Kupari forward command post on the 5th of December. In September 2003, on page 113 of his interview, Jokic said that on the 5th of December 1991, there had been a briefing at the Kupari forward command post. Witness Jokic said that he personally chaired the briefing. Jokic said in his interview in July 2002 that after the negotiations in Cavtat, he went directly to Kumbor. This is on page 185. At his examination-in-chief on the 23rd of July 2004, Jokic said that he went to Trebinje after the negotiations in Cavtat. Then he said that he went from Trebinje to Kupari, and then from Kupari to Kumbor. The discrepancies in his description of his movements after the negotiations in Cavtat are explained by Jokic by saying that he consulted officers from the 9th VPS after the 1st of July 2001, and they told him what his movements had been on that day. In 2002, Witness Jokic said that he went to Kumbor from Cavtat. In 2004, he says that from Cavtat, he went to Trebinje. In 2003 he said that he personally chaired the briefing on the 5th of December in Kupari, and in 2004, he said that there had been no briefing at all whatsoever in Kupari on the 5th of December. Jokic is giving a false description of events in order to conceal his own role in them. Also, in connection with the 5th of December, Witness Hvalkof in his report noted down the results of the negotiations of which he had been informed by Minister Rudolf. There is mention here that a cease-fire was considered which was to take effect 24 hours after the signing of the agreement. When Witness Rudolf was shown this document, P61, item 29, he confirmed that the document faithfully reflects the substance of the meeting held in Cavtat on the 5th of December. Witness Rudolf did not mention anywhere in his testimony that on the 5th of December an absolute cease-fire had been agreed on for the following day at 1200 hours. From the war log of the 9th VPS, it is evident that the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff demanded that the vessel Argosy be allowed to pass through for the negotiations in Cavtat and that passage was granted to this vessel carrying the negotiators. The Prosecution pointed out that this showed that Jokic had nothing to do with planning the attack on Srdj because he had sent a message granting leave for the negotiators to travel, but it is obvious that he would not have informed them of the forthcoming attack. He did not, however, grant permission for local line boats to sail, nor did he allow the French vessel to sail into the port. I have already stated that the regular combat report of the 9th VPS does not contain anything about the negotiations in Cavtat or anything about the absolute cease-fire on the 6th of December. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the command of the 9th VPS in its regular combat report of the 7th states under item 2 that negotiations were continued with represent --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it reports that these negotiations were attended personally by the commander and the negotiations were carried out in Cavtat. Under item 3 of that report, the column which says "I decided," I quote "strictly comply with the agreed cease-fire, inform the staff of all units about the cease-fire which has to be abided by strictly." No similarity between the ways in which the ordered cease-fire is notified, between the cease-fire for the 5th of December, D111, and between D61, the routine manner in which such cease-fires are ordered. No similarity whatsoever. By reviewing the evidence, we can see that no cease-fire was agreed for the 6th of December, and that Jokic was allegedly -- correction, that Jokic did not inform the superior command about the alleged cease-fire, nor did he inform his own units. Designating the cease-fire for the 6th of December at 1200 hours was to have been a deadline for the command of the 9th VPS to carry out the planned attack on Srdj. Your Honours have heard from witnesses Nesic and Stojanovic that on the 5th of December, a briefing was held at the forward command post, or rather, at Ivanica, and this was chaired by the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. All the witnesses say that at that meeting, they were informed by the commander that the attack -- an attack on Srdj on the 6th of December had been ordered and approved, and that the unit would receive artillery support from Cilipi, from 130-millimetre guns, as well as support from the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade which was at Osojnik. At that meeting, a detailed plan of attack was established. Assault groups were designated, directions of attack, preparations for the attack were outlined. Witness Lemal asked for the necessary materiel for the attack on the 6th of December. Explosives, flak jackets, stun grenades, and it was the chief of staff of the 9th VPS personally who brought this materiel to him. This was Captain Zec who, on that occasion, spoke to the men who were to take part in the attack. These preparations were testified to by witnesses Stojanovic, Pesic, and Jovica Nesic. And we have dealt with -- in detail with this in our closing brief. The commander of the 130-millimetre gun battery said that on the 5th of December, his commander had given him the task of being at Zarkovica at 6.00 on the following day in order to provide support to the 3rd Battalion and that he was to be resubordinated to Captain Kovacevic. He pointed out that the observation post at Zarkovica was manned only when an operation was planned and when it was necessary to guide the fire. From the report on the logistics of the 9th VPS command of the 5th December, it is evident that on that day Kupari was replenished with 10 kilograms of plastic explosives, stun grenades, and so on. Another report of the 4th of December shows that the 3rd Battalion was replenished with mortar shells, Maljutkas, and gun ammunition, as well as tank grenades. It is evident from these reports that immediately before the attack, the 3rd Battalion was replenished with materiel and equipment which can only be used to carry out the task of taking a fortified facility. The attack on Srdj began on the morning of the 6th of December after preparation of fire was carried out, or rather preparation of the attack. Fire was opened from ZIS guns and mortars, and these are guns which were retained by the command of the 9th VPS until the problem of Srdj was solved. During the infantry attack on Srdj, there were soldiers from the 3rd Battalion who were killed. The Croatian forces opened fire from all parts of Dubrovnik on Srdj defending that facility, and Defence witnesses testified to this in detail. Minister Rudolf said that on the 6th of December 1991, he was awakened by gunfire. He tried to get through to Jokic. First he got his secretary, then Jokic himself. And he told him that fire had been opened on Dubrovnik. He says that Jokic proposed a cease-fire over the telephone starting at 1100 hours and said that he was Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond investigating what was going on. However, from the log of Witness Hvalkof, we can see that the shelling began from land and sea in the direction of the Srdj fortress at 6.00 in the morning, and a similar message was sent by the crisis staff to the 9th VPS saying that fire was being opened from tanks, mortars, and naval artillery on Dubrovnik. In the war log at 06.50, there is an entry whereby Kovacevic says that mortar fire has been opened on Srdj. Witness Drljan said that at about 07.15, he had received an order from Commander Jokic which was transmitted to him by Zec that he should go to Zarkovica and transmit the order to Kovacevic that he was not to fire on the Old Town. From the radio log of the Dubrovnik Port Authority of the 6th of December, a message was received in the morning for Minister Rudolf at 805 hours from the VPS Boka. It is said that VPS is making efforts to stop the clash because fire had been opened from Srdj and Lapad. And he asked -- or rather, the VPS asked that Minister Rudolf intervene at once, that the hostilities be -- that the hostilities end at 11.15. Why should the hostilities end two hours after the message had been sent? Because the plan was that Srdj should be taken through a fast operation, and it was assumed that this would be sufficient time, regardless of the Croatian resistance, to complete the operation successfully, especially bearing in mind that Defence witnesses said, and this is confirmed by the war log of the 9th VPS, that there is no order, not a single order of the 6th of December that the attack on Srdj should be halted and that the units should withdraw to their starting positions. The war log contains, among other things, detailed communication that carried on during the attack on Srdj between the superior command and the subordinated units taking part in the attack. From the war log, we see that Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic from Osojnik as early as 8.36 had given a specification of targets and the expenditure of ammunition in the action against Dubrovnik targets. We can also see that readiness of 130-millimetre cannons had been ordered. Not only did Kovacevic receive no orders from anybody to withdraw, but the operative centre was following the situation very closely. He was receiving messages from Zec, Jovanovic, and other protagonists in the action against Srdj. At 2.00, Kovacevic messages that he had another two bunkers to deal with, that fire was being opened against them from the town. That's at 12.00. At 11.50, the operative centre was informed that Srdj had not fallen yet, that the National Guards Corps members were resisting strongly from houses and that they would open fire from tanks, rocket launchers, and use hand grenades. At 13.15 on the 6th of December, the operations centre transmits the order of the commander of the 9th VPS to open fire only against Srdj, to refrain from shooting at the city. That message was issued, or rather transmitted to Kovacevic, issued originally by Jokic, by Zec. Around 1400 hours that day, Captain Kovacevic informs the operations centre that he was thinking about pulling back his people from Mount Srdj because they were exhausted and they were cold. At that moment, also nobody from the command of the 9th VPS ordered them to stop the attack. At 14.45, Kovacevic again informs the forward command post at Kupari that his situation at Srdj was becoming untenable and that he was seeking approval to withdraw his men. Only then did the command of the 9th VPS give Kovacevic approval to pull back his men. That means that until that time, 14.45, he hadn't been given that approval, and that coincides with our submissions because in the war log we find no orders about discontinuing the attack and withdrawing the troops from Mount Srdj. Again, at 15.20, Kovacevic informs the command that he had withdrawn and that they were at that time firing on Mount Srdj from mortars. Witness Jokic claimed that he was unable to contact Kovacevic, that allegedly the lines were down, that there was no connection. But it is an obvious untruth because all communications of the 9th VPS and the 3rd Battalion were in perfect working order on that day. That was confirmed by the witnesses and that is confirmed by the war log of the 9th VPS itself. The chief of staff of the 9th VPS, all the way until the end of the operation, continues to be in Zarkovica next to Captain Kovacevic. And even at Kovacevic's request, he demanded explosives from the engineering unit to be delivered to them. Such a message was sent at 12.30. In that war log for the entry -- Your Honours, maybe I am speaking too fast. But my colleague is telling me that a number of dates and times were recorded incorrectly, and we should pay attention to that in the transcript. In the war log for the 6th of December, there is an entry in the afternoon hours that the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade was firing from 15.45 to 16.15 from 120-millimetre mortars against Sustjepan. That means that Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic, just like earlier that morning, was informing the superior command of the actions underway. In that same war log, we see that Admiral Jokic, at 14.15, took off from Cilipi airfield towards Belgrade. He was going to report to the federal secretary for national defence, Kadijevic. I will now turn to the investigation related to the events of the 6th of December. After that meeting where he reported to Kadijevic, Jokic made a report on the 7th of December about the action against Mount Srdj launched by the 3rd Battalion and submitted it to General Simonovic. That day, in that report he designated Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic and Kovacevic as very capable officers. That's D65. In point 1(b), he described the situation around Mount Srdj, the deployment of forces of the 3rd Battalion, the strength of MUP forces and the ZNG, and he described also the firing provocations against the 3rd Battalion. He wrote that as of the 6th of December at midnight, the 2nd and 3rd Companies of the 3rd Battalion were under constant machine-gun, sniper, and occasionally anti-aircraft gunfire from Mount Srdj which killed one soldier and wounded another. However, from the war log of the 9th VPS, we do not see any reference to anything of the kind. Jokic testified that on the 6th of December at 0445 hours, he was awakened by Kozaric who informed him that there was one soldier killed. Transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He also testified that at 4.45 on that same day, he was informed - only informed by Kozaric - that fire had been opened against the 3rd Battalion. Page 4.880. After that, Jokic testified that he had been informed that morning at 6.00 about the losses, again, by Kozaric. In the report to the General Staff, D65 of 7 December, Jokic wrote that until the start of the attack, one soldier of the 3rd Battalion was killed, another was wounded. In cross-examination on the 16th April of this year, he stated that none of this was true and that nobody had been killed or wounded either before 06.45 or later on the 6th of December. The Defence wishes to emphasise here that until the 16th of April, in five earlier interviews in the past two years and in cross-examination as well -- examination-in-chief and even at the beginning of cross-examination, he always kept saying that the 3rd Battalion on that morning, at 06.45, had one soldier killed and one wounded. He could not tell anyone why he was changing his testimony. Furthermore, in his report to the General Staff, Jokic writes that the commander of the 3rd Battalion, after assessing that the fire was lethal to the unit, as part of improving their tactical position, he made the decision to attack Mount Srdj. It is an obviously untruthful report to the General Staff about the events of the 6th of December. In this way, Jokic wishes to evade his own responsibility for the events. Numerous witnesses, Miroslav Jovanovic, Lemal, Stojanovic, Nesic, Sikimic, as well as a series of documents exhibited in this case, primarily D108, Jovanovic's report, as well as the war log are evidence directly indicating that the attack on Srdj had been planned and approved by the command of the 9th VPS. There is a vast quantity of other evidence pointing to the same conclusion. Further on in the report to the General Staff, he says that nobody had approved the action against Srdj, that he was acting according to the general plan of action which included an attack on Srdj. Witness Jokic himself stated before the Court that there was never an aspiration or an assignment to capture Srdj. However, we had witnesses who confirmed that the attack had been approved. We can see that the ZIS cannons could not be taken away from the 3rd Battalion before the Srdj problem was resolved, and that capturing Srdj was Jokic's objective. In November 1991, we see from Exhibits P118, P126, and D57, from these exhibits we see that it was precisely the 3rd Battalion which was tasked with taking Mount Srdj. But we see no evidence that the 2nd Operational Group had ever issued an order to take Mount Srdj. This is the subject of an order of the military naval district of the 20th December 1991. It's Exhibit P199. Furthermore, in his report to the General Staff of the 7th of December, Jokic incorrectly describes the activities undertaken by the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic where he says that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to repeat something that did not enter the transcript. Witness Jokic wrote in that report that Jovanovic had discontinued fire at 1115 hours. Jokic made an untruthful report to the General Staff because he continues in that report to state that units of the 9th VPS had complied with the agreed cease-fire at 1115 hours on the 6th of December. In the same report to the General Staff, Jokic states that the 3rd Battalion had remained at Srdj until 14.35 when it was decided to pull out the unit from Srdj and take it back to its point of departure. However, he fails to report to the General Staff who it was who decided to pull back the 3rd Battalion. In the same report, Jokic says -- states at 1600 hours, five hours after a cease-fire according to the statement of Minister Rudolf, the Orthodox church in the Old Town and a number of other houses were on fire. First of all, it was untrue that for five hours, the units of the 9th VPS did not open fire. We can see that from the war log and other evidence. Second, Jokic untruthfully reported the damage in the Old Town to the General Staff because in that time, Minister Rudolf had sent several messages describing specific damage and specific damaged facilities in the Old Town. In addition to that, his own chief of staff Zec spent the entire day at Zarkovica. In that same report to the General Staff, Jokic says that Miroslav Jovanovic was removed, stating no reasons for his removal, which shows that he had full authority to remove a battalion commander and initiate an investigation. Jokic would not have needed anyone's approval or consent in order to remove Miroslav Jovanovic which he did immediately. In addition to which, Jokic informed the General Staff that he had initiated an investigation and that he would soon be taking further measures. From that moment on, no one could restrict his right and powers to conduct that investigation or hamper that investigation because he received his tasks in Belgrade. Witness Jokic said that as soon as the 6th of December in the evening, he interviewed and took a written statement from Zec, from Colonel Kovacevic, and from Kozaric, whereas he did not interview Captain Kovacevic. Witness Jovica Nesic confirmed that on the 8th of December, together with Battalion Commander Kovacevic, he Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond was at the Kupari forward command post. The company commander Jeremic was also with him, and Nesic and Jeremic together drew up a written report on the operations of the 6th of December. Having learned that Lieutenant Colonel Kovacevic had already submitted his report to the operations centre by 1400 hours, it is quite obvious that Jokic was in a position to view the war log, and it is quite obvious that he did, in fact, use it while drafting his report to the General Staff. What happened later on the 8th of December? Officers Boskovic and Pesic were dispatched to Dubrovnik with a cameraman to record what had happened in the Old Town. They brought back a report and some footage that they recorded in Dubrovnik. Jokic viewed these back at his command post in Kumbor. Therefore, all of these previous activities that I have just enumerated indicate that Jokic did, in fact, carry out an alleged investigation into the events on the 6th of December, and this investigation was done between the 6th and the 9th of December. On the 9th of December, Jokic forwards his conclusions to the deputy federal secretary for national defence, Admiral Brovet. Here I wish to point out that this was an interim report which he submitted directly to the federal secretary. Damage was described that had been ascertained when touring the Old Town. Further, it was underlined that the damage to cultural and historical monuments was not significant. It was also stated that it could not be ascertained where the damage had come from or who it was caused by. And what is more indicative, that the perpetrators could not be named since it was obvious that much of the damage did not stem from attacks that had come from outside the Old Town, which means that the damage that came about was probably as a result of fighting that went on inside the Old Town, in Jokic's understanding, or at least that was the way he reported to the supreme command. While doing this, he has certain knowledge of how damage in the Old Town came about. If nothing else, it was only in the previous day that Jovica Nesic had submitted a written report where among other things he discussed targets that were, in fact, targeted, that were inside the Old Town. Based on these allegations that he made in the report, it is quite obvious that Jokic then ended the investigation. This report was signed by him personally, and it was dispatched to Belgrade. This is an unambiguous document which unequivocally stems from the commander of the 9th VPS as confirmed before this Trial Chamber by General Zorc, an OTP expert witness. The Defence wishes to point out that the investigation that Jokic brought to an end was done and carried out unbeknownst to General Strugar, and General Strugar was kept in the dark about its progress and results. The outcome of that alleged investigation was certainly influenced by Jokic's attempt to conceal what happened on the 6th of December as well as his own role and the extent of his involvement in what happened. It was entirely cynical of Jokic to say, when he viewed the footage that was marked P145, the inspection of the Old Town, that the impression he had now was much clearer and much stronger than when he originally viewed this footage back at his command in Kumbor in 1991. The report dated the 9th of December was not submitted to the 2nd Operational Group, nor was the report dated the 7th of December, the one that was sent to the General Staff. Those two reports are in reference to the 6th of December 1991. It was on account of that that Jokic was called to see the general secretary personally. It was quite obvious that he was tasked with reporting personally to the military leadership and to shed light on the causes, progress, and consequences of the operation on Srdj. It is clear simply because these reports were not sent to the 2nd Operational Group. It is also quite obvious that Jokic received a special task to draw up those reports. Those would have been regular and perfectly usual reports that would have had to go through the normal and usual channels of command and reporting. However, the reports were not submitted to the 2nd Operational Group, not even as simply for their information. As for the causes, progress, and results of the operation, there was direct communication between Jokic, the SSNO, and the General Staff which was the supreme level of command in the JNA. The command of the 2nd Operational Group was entirely left out. Jokic acted on orders that he had received from the supreme command of the JNA. He had no duty to inform the command of the 2nd Operational Group, and he took advantage of not being duty-bound to inform them. However, not even their regular combat reports that were dated the 7th of December contain even a shred of information on what his command actually did about what transpired on the 6th of December, nor do these contain any indication whatsoever that he had informed the General Staff about that. The Defence would like to underline the fact that the General Staff has every right to communicate directly and hand out tasks and missions directly bypassing the directly superior commands which this example very clearly illustrates. The Defence would like to point out that in our brief, we commented at length on the communication between federal secretary Kadijevic, his deputy Brovet, and international diplomats who asked questions about what happened on the 6th of December.
