utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, the Defence would now like to briefly comment on persons that were referred to as victims on the 6th of December 1991 as stated in this third amended indictment. First of all, a person that was allegedly wounded as a civilian on the 6th of December 1991, Mato Valjalo. In our brief, we provided numerous arguments, forensic and medical arguments, as well as formal and legal arguments in relation to this witness and the facts surrounding his injury. Now, I would only like to say that Mato Valjalo, as he stated himself, drove members of the crisis staff, municipal officials, and Croatian leaders to their war tasks. Therefore, he was not a driver. He was a person who was actively involved in every way in the general war effort by driving other persons to their war assignments. What is important here is that these facts were established by bodies working for the Dubrovnik and Neretva county, or more specifically their defence administration. It's the local defence administration that informs us of his role and his status at times relevant to the indictment. Bearing in mind this written evidence and other documents that I will not go into now, the Defence believes if indeed this person was wounded in the Old Town on the 6th of December, it was certainly not as a civilian. He was going about his usual daily tasks at the time. And based on this, we see that his tasks were related to the war effort. This comes across with great clarity based on the documents that he himself produced before this Trial Chamber. In relation to Witness Vlasica, there are various inconsistencies in his testimony of which I would like to point out the following, Your Honours, because I believe it can easily be commented now. Witness Vlasica, first of all, Your Honours, tells us that he was hit in the foot. And after that, he tells us that it was, in fact, the right upper leg and not the foot. All the other medical documents issued by the hospital, as well as the case history in relation to his injury, indicate that a person name Ivo Vlasica was, in fact, wounded in the left upper leg, which is very noteworthy. Your Honours, I am talking about D71, evidence before the Trial Chamber. There was a ruling by the Dubrovnik municipal court against Zeljko Soldo in relation to events of the 6th of December. The ruling says that based on information provided by the emergency service of the St. Blaise hospital in Dubrovnik, the information used to ascertain which persons exactly were wounded or killed in Dubrovnik on that day, the injured person was indeed Ivo Vlasica. However, this is not a middle-aged man. This is, in fact, a child that was born in 1987. You can see that in the ruling, and you can also see it on page 16 of the sentence that I have referred to. As for persons that were referred to as persons who were killed on the 6th of December, I would like to point out that based on P70, it is impossible to ascertain the cause and time of their deaths. These two elements are indispensable for the Trial Chamber to be established beyond reasonable doubt in order to be able to take these persons into account as persons who were really killed as stated in the indictment. Exhibit P70 is a record of the external examination drawn up by Dr. Ciganovic who appeared as a witness before the Trial Chamber. As for the much-debated damage and in relation to positions put forward by OTP witnesses testifying to that damage and its extent, the Defence would like to point out a severe discrepancy between their positions and their recollection in relation to what happened in Dubrovnik. Those are really witnesses, the so-called crime-base witnesses. And what strikes us as important in relation to those witnesses is that these people in their description of events paint a picture for us that does not seem to be consistent with what was going on at the time. There is a certain pattern that emerges. All these witnesses were not aware of Croatian military presence in or around the town of Dubrovnik. They never heard of anything like that. On the other hand, we have crime-base witnesses, and those witnesses refer to damage inside the Old Town and testify to it in a way that, to say the least, was exaggerated, overblown, and inaccurate. Your Honours, you heard the testimony of Mr. Jusic, the person who was a member of the crisis staff. But he appears to be unaware of something that the entire town knew; namely, that there were Croatian positions on Mount Srdj. The only thing that Witness Jusic knows about the Croatian forces is what he heard on Radio Montenegro. What's more, Mr. Jusic only seemed to find out that his brother actually lived in Dubrovnik here in The Hague and that he actually was a member of the Croatian forces in late 1991. He appears not to have been familiar with that at the time. The same goes for Lucianja Peko in her statement dated 2000 for the OTP, she mentioned nothing. But here before the Trial Chamber, she referred to guns, Croatian guns, although suddenly she said there were no guns and although she lived in Dubrovnik she never saw a single Croatian soldier or a single Croatian position inside the Old Town. The defence line ran adjacent to her house. For some reason, however, and I'm only naming a couple of very striking examples, but the same applies to a number of other witnesses from the same OTP witness group, she seems to have seen nothing at all; none of that at least. Witness Grubasic likewise claims to have seen nothing. Now, those facts, all this conscious disregard of what appeared to be well-known facts sheds a different light on their testimonies in their entirety. It makes them appear unreliable and not trustworthy and certainly as constituting no basis for the Trial Chamber to ascertain the extent of damage to the Old Town. If you will please merely remember Witness Vukovic, Your Honours, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond who spoke before this Trial Chamber about something that shocked him, mainly when he saw his mother's house after the 6th of December 1991. The next day, he personally carried out an inspection in that area and in the area where his mother's house was. However, the damage that he was stunned by, the damage that shocked him and which part in that damage was actually due to his own activity was passed over in silence. He was asked to specify where exactly his mother's house was, but he couldn't. The facts, however, in that case are undeniable. Of the six buildings which allegedly were gutted due to the activities of the JNA on the 6th of December, as many as five were owned or had been owned by persons from Serbia or Montenegro. This is not a spurious claim. It is something that is grounded in video footage and in what the witness who helped us analyse the video footage testified before the Trial Chamber. The ground floor of the Grbic house is where a shop owned by the Beko [phoen] Company of Belgrade was gutted. In another one was a shop belonging to Titex from Titograd. A third one belonged to Kluz [phoen]. The fourth one was across the road from the Serbian Orthodox church, and it was a shop belonging to a Serb, as Djelo Jusic said. Witness Ogresta testifying about the fifth building in question said that on the ground floor, there was a shop belonging to a company from Belgrade. Out of the six buildings that were gutted, five were either owned by or had connections with persons from Serbia and Montenegro. The Defence sees more than pure coincidence in this fact. Finally, in connection with the evidence following from the preliminary report on war damage in Dubrovnik and the persons who compiled that report, the Defence wishes to point out that these persons were not trained to do this job, that no photographs were taken or sketches made, that nothing was established about the way the damage was inflicted, nothing was established about the direction from which the shell arrived, nothing was done by way of an on-the-spot investigation by the police. These persons simply looked at these houses for a few minutes and then noted down both the time of the damage, the origin of the damage, and so on. Witness Peko looked at 11 buildings in the space of four hours. The Defence believes that this evidence on damage which was introduced through the testimony of Witnesses Peko, Kaiser, and Vukovic cannot be viewed as credible, and there are abundant facts both in our filing and in our cross-examination, our extensive cross-examination which prove this. Your Honours, bearing in mind my time limitations, I will simply make a few points about some topics. An artillery expert called by the Defence, Janko Vilicic, based on precise and thorough research and investigation mentioned the following in his report, among other things: First of all, the Old Town was never the primary target of the JNA units in any situation or at any time. If some projectiles did land in the Old Town, it was as a result of the deployment of the Croatian forces and their firing on the units of the JNA. It is especially noteworthy that Vilicic says that the minimum distance of Croatian positions which would not have imperilled the Old Town would have been 500 metres from the walls of the Old Town. The Defence also asks Your Honours to take into consideration a fact that we find indisputable, and that is what Dr. Vilicic said here about a shell falling in front of the church of St. Blaise and the Sponza Palace. Dr. Vilicic conducted an analysis of the traces and of footage made immediately in the aftermath of the event, and he concluded that the shell arrived from a direction where there were no JNA positions. Your Honours, the Defence of General Strugar submits that the accused Strugar is not guilty on any of the counts of the amended indictment. For the sake of caution, the Defence of General Strugar wishes to point to significant mitigating factors should the Trial Chamber find General Strugar guilty of any of the counts of the third amended indictment that he is charged with. First of all, Your Honours, what must be taken into account is the degree of participation of General Strugar in the events that he is charged with. Strugar did not participate actively in this event in any way. The events took place without his knowledge and contrary to his orders. During the course of the operation itself, Jokic did not inform Strugar about it because he felt that would have been a waste of time. And this has already been mentioned today. The Defence wishes to point out that any human victim is much to be regretted by all, as is any material damage. However, the Defence must stress on this occasion that the victims and consequences General Strugar is charged with as well as the damage that has been spoken of here cannot be compared in any way with the other cases before this International Tribunal. This is something that must certainly be taken into account should this case come to the sentencing stage. It is especially important to note that immediately after the events on the 7th of December 1991, he -- General Strugar expressed his regrets and apologies to Minister Rudolf occasioned by the event of 6th of December 1991. The regret was expressed immediately following the event which is the subject of the indictment, and this fact must have great significance in any possible sentencing of the accused, General Strugar. It is especially significant that General Strugar surrendered voluntarily to this Tribunal, and he announced his intention the day after the publication of his indictment in early October 2001. The Defence also requests that the Trial Chamber, should it find that General Strugar is guilty under any of the counts, should take into account the family situation of General Strugar, which is described in greater detail in our final brief. This also relates to the good character of the accused. In the view of the Defence, in this case, the Trial Chamber should create a precedent with regard to the weight to be attached to the health, age, and family situation of the accused. In no other case before the Tribunal where this kind of argument has been put forward were there such strong arguments for a possible sentence to be mitigated to the greatest possible extent. General Strugar has very serious health problems to which special attention should be paid during sentencing. There are many indisputable diagnoses of General Strugar ranging from dementia, kidney problems, and orthopedic problems. Prosecution experts, when General Strugar's ability to stand trial was being evaluated, never questioned the existence of these conditions, but only their effect on his fitness to stand trial. Also, the psychological problems related to dementia should be taken into account as well as his serious kidney condition on which an expert's report shall be submitted, drawn up by Dr. Savo Micic. Another point to be taken into account are the problems General Strugar has with his neck vertebrae and his hips, and these have been dealt with in the expert report of Dr. Vuckovic [phoen]. When evaluating all these facts, Your Honours, one must bear in mind the purpose of sentencing. One must bear in mind that the purpose of sentencing should not be pure retribution, which would be the case were a long sentence to be imposed. Should General Strugar be sentenced, the purpose of prevention has already been achieved. As for general prevention, a person who is 71 years of age, this can be achieved by a minimum sentence should the Chamber find that any sentence at all should be imposed on General Strugar. Your Honours, my colleague Rodic will now address you on the final points to be put forward by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have limited time available, and therefore I would only briefly like to draw Your Honours' attention to Witness Colm Doyle, a Prosecution witness who, in the view of the Defence, said only one true thing in relation to the meeting of the 6th of December and the attack of the paramilitary formations in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the units of the 2nd Operational Group around the area of Neum, not those around Dubrovnik. This has been recorded in the logbook of Witness Svicevic, which is also a contemporaneous document and a reliable one where no mention is made at all of any orders to shell Dubrovnik. I also wish to draw Your Honours' attention in connection with this witness to the extensive cross-examination of Witness Doyle who was unable to provide satisfactory replies and was contradictory in his statements. I also wish to point out to Your Honours what the Prosecution witness Zorc said, as well as Svicevic and Colm Doyle, Witness Zorc and his testimony has been dealt with in detail in the Defence brief, and I only wish briefly to point out that Witness Zorc during his cross-examination confirmed the Defence case and everything put forward by the Defence in connection with the military documents and the behaviour of the command of the 9th VPS in the critical situation on the eve of the 6th of December and on the 6th of December 1991, which he characterised as "contrary to the then-valid doctrine of command in the JNA". Also, in view of what was said by my colleague, I wish to draw your attention to a general characteristic of this trial in relation to the Prosecution case. Everything my colleague said about the witnesses should be taken into consideration. It was quite unrealistic that these witnesses should say they knew nothing and had no information about the existence of Croatian military forces in Dubrovnik. It was also obvious that the Prosecution insisted that their witnesses should, as far as weapons, soldiers, and positions of the Croatian side in or near the Old Town, that they should dislocate these, and this went so far that the commander of the defence of Dubrovnik, looking at document P160 on which positions were marked, and probably they did not know that this map would ever reach the Tribunal, the positions of Croatian artillery pieces were marked there in 1991, and then Witness Negodic moved all the positions that were near the Old Town. He said that they were not operational on the 6th of December. Bogosica Park, Gradac, Lovrijenac, Lazareti, a hundred metres from the Old Town near the Ploce gate, that is, everything that could imperil the Old Town. The most characteristic point was when a mark designating anti-aircraft weapons north of the Old Town, in its immediate vicinity, was pointed out, and Witness Negodic invented a statement saying that it was the top of the arrow that showed where this weapon was, only so that he could represent it as being outside the Old Town. The Prosecution expert, Lieutenant Colonel Poje who is an artillery man by his military profession in the same way tried to move this position, to dislocate it, but he moved it to a distance of 300 metres from the Old Town. During the cross-examination, he brought it closer. He brought it to a distance of a hundred metres. And as for the position of the cable car, we know what the distance was even if it was a position. However, Prosecution Witness Zorc, who is also a professional, a graduate of the top military schools, the command staff academy, and the academy of the air defence, said according to the instructions on the drawing of military maps, the centre of a symbol designates the position of a piece or a weapon, and he was very surprised when told about the testimony according to which allegedly only the tip of the symbol designated the position of artillery pieces rather than the centre of the symbol. I would try, Your Honours, in conclusion, to present to you the conclusions and submissions of our Defence; namely, Witness Jokic very Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond suddenly in early December received instructions and the task to conclude a cease-fire agreement urgently with the highest representatives of the Croatian side. However, Witness Jokic had not resolved the problem of Mount Srdj which was obviously a thorn in his side, as we could see from the previous parts of our final trial brief. The time needed for negotiations was long, and the problem of Srdj needed to be resolved. That is why the Witness Jokic delayed negotiations with the representatives of Croatia on the 5th of December, justifying it with an insignificant pretext. The difference in strength between the units blocking Dubrovnik and those attacking from Mount Srdj was obvious. Witness Jokic believed that in a very short time, he would be able to resolve the problem of Srdj before the comprehensive cease-fire scheduled for 6th December. Witness testimony and other evidence indicate and confirm that without the knowledge of the superior command of the 2nd Operational Group, the action of attack on Srdj organised in a textbook manner was planned and mounted. The units had the task to neutralise the firing position of Croatian forces in Dubrovnik that could possibly counterattack. It is quite certain that in the context of the agreed cease-fire and the expected signing of the agreement, the attack on Mount Srdj would cause vehement reactions, primarily on the Croatian side. However, Witness Jokic took it upon himself to deal with the problem because in the military hierarchy, there is a huge difference between a vice-admiral occupying the position of corps commander and lower ranks such as battalion commanders who were designated to implement the action of capturing Mount Srdj. Why is Jokic's theory on a self-initiated attack on Srdj unbelievable? First of all, because the instruction on the work of command staff, a forward command post is organised only when the commander is no longer able to perform his duties in relation to units from his basic command post. In that case, the commander, together with some of his command staff, goes to the forward command post from which he discharges his duties of command and control. From the 9th VPS command, Jokic chose himself, Zec, assistant for land forces Kovacevic, and head of the operations -- head of operations Kozaric. The fundamental principle of the command doctrine is as follows: From a forward command post or a point from which direct control is exercised, there is staff able to take decisions at every moment, which means that at any time there had to be either the commander or the chief of staff at the forward command post. In this case, on the 5th and 6th December, that had to be Lieutenant Colonel Kovacevic. However, at that time, not only were Jokic, Zec, and Kovacevic absent from that forward command post, but nobody, even their own operations officer Kozaric, could even find them. Beginning with 6.00 on the 6th of December, according to the war log, on the 6th of December at 1349 hours, a search was going on in Bileca for Kovacevic. At 14.45, a message came notifying of one dead and one wounded, whereas the commander of the corps continued allegedly to sleep. On that day, on the same day when he was supposed to sign a comprehensive cease-fire agreement, it is unbelievable that in the period from 4.45 in the morning to 6.00 when he allegedly received a call from the forward command post and the notification that the 3rd Battalion was going to attack Srdj he did not receive either directly or through the chief of staff or Kovacevic such information or tried to prevent that self-willed attack. Furthermore, if it was indeed an attack initiated by the 3rd Battalion itself, it is unbelievable that the war log for the 6th of December does not contain a single entry from which it would be evident that such an attack was banned and that a withdrawal of units was ordered. Furthermore, it is incredible that among four colonels, including the chief of staff, assistant commander for land forces, and others were unable to stop that self-willed attack mounted by the battalion commander for seven hours. I emphasise that those four do not include the two designated by Jokic, Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic or Gojko Djurasic. It is even less believable that from 4.45 in the morning all the way up to 1400 hours in a situation where this self-willed attack was going on, the commander of the 9th VPS did not appear at his own forward command post or even at the location where the commander of the 3rd Battalion was in order to stop that attack. It is incredible that from early morning hours until late in the afternoon, the commander of the 9th VPS had no information whatsoever and didn't know that in the combat activities on the 6th of December the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade was involved as well. This battalion in its own activities and fire actions did inform in detail the operations centre of the 9th VPS in Kupari. All this is unbelievable because Jokic himself says that he had unhindered communication with the operations centre in Kupari. It is incredible that Jokic and his command failed to inform the superior command, that is, the 2nd Operational Group, of this self-willed attack mounted by the commander of the 3rd Battalion. And we have to bear in mind that Jokic qualifies any such suggestion as a pure waste of time. It is incredible that Jokic stopped the attack by the 3rd Battalion while allowing at the same time the battalion to fire from its artillery pieces at 13.05 on the 6th of December. It is incredible that the commander should stop this so-called self-willed attack while at 1330 hours, the commander was requesting engineering staff with explosives for purposes of the attack, whereas the chief of staff whom Jokic allegedly again sent to stop the attack orders that these explosives be made available to the battalion commander without delay. It is incredible and inexplicable that due to this allegedly self-initiated attack which had very heavy consequences, after submitting a report to the General Staff, no measures were allowed in order to replace the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. It is also incredible and inexplicable bearing all this in mind that the system of command of the 9th VPS could fail to such an extent to prohibit and put an end to this self-willed attack mounted on Mount Srdj by the commander of the 3rd Battalion on the 6th of December. We see a completely different role played by the commander of the 9th VPS regarding the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December. On the 5th of December, namely, after the negotiations in Cavtat were ended, he ordered the chief of the General Staff to prohibit Cape Africa from entering the harbour. On the same day, he prohibited that approval should be given to three smaller vessels to enter the port in which prior communication was completely normal, whereas these vessels were carrying humanitarian aid. Furthermore, the command of the 9th VPS at the command post in Kupari from 0650 to 1620 hours on the 6th of December contacted the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade on at least 11 occasions. That was Captain Kovacevic. In none of these contacts do we find any orders to Kovacevic to withdraw his units and return them to their initial position. Furthermore, the commander of the 9th VPS, and this is a fact, ordered and allowed the commander of the 3rd Battalion to use mortars against Srdj. The chief of staff of the 9th VPS visited the position of the 3rd Battalion commander Kovacevic and did not give him orders to stop the attack and withdraw his unit. How should he, if he participated himself on the 5th of December in the planning and approval of this attack? The chief of staff, precisely for this reason, ordered explosives to be made available to this commander in order to attack Srdj. The commander of the 9th VPS, Jokic, for the duration of the attack on Srdj spoke early in the morning at the command post in Cavtat with the chief of staff of the 9th VPS, and they left the command post together. Communications in Cavtat functioned well. The telephones in Cavtat worked. There were no radio or radio relay problems as Jokic would have us believe. The command of the 9th VPS was informed on the 4th of December of the arrival of Croatian negotiators. On the 4th of December, the command of the 9th VPS reinforced the 3rd Battalion with ammunition for mortars, anti-tank Maljutka grenades. The command of the 9th VPS replenished the forward command post at Kupari with explosives that were completely unnecessary for staff work at a forward command post. They gave them AGF or shock -- stun grenades. On the 6th of December, the commander of the 9th VPS took off from Cilipi going to Podgorica and Belgrade at 14.15, whereas at 14.45, the 9th VPS only then approved the withdrawal of Kovacevic from Srdj. In their regular combat report dated the 5th of December, the command of the VPS did not report on the negotiations in Cavtat. On the 6th of December, the operations centre at the Kupari forward command post did not inform the 2nd Operational Group about the attack against Srdj. The European Mission and the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff at 0612 hours in the morning of the 6th of December informed the VPS about the attack at Srdj and fire being opened. On that same day at 0855 hours, the Boka VPS sends a message to Minister Rudolf telling him that they're doing their best to stop the attack. It is only two-and-a-half hours later that the cease-fire should come into effect. At 10.27 on the 6th of December, Minister Rudolf receives a message in which Witness Jokic invites him to a meeting as soon as possible, he said, because later he would be busy, as indeed he was because he was called over by General Kadijevic, as Witness Handzijev testified. At 11.05 the Crisis Staff issues a denial of any activity by the Croatian forces based on Srdj or in Lapad. At 11.28, Minister Rudolf informs Jokic that the units are still manoeuvring on Srdj despite the cease-fire that had been agreed. At 11.45, Minister Rudolf receives a message from Admiral Jokic telling him that General Kadijevic demanded a serious investigation and informing Rudolf that he would soon be on his way to Belgrade to see Kadijevic, proposing that they meet again for talks on the 7th of December and that ships should be checked inside the Gruz harbour. On the 7th of December, the commander of the 9th VPS drew up a report on the progress of the operation against Srdj and forwarded this report to the General Staff. This report contradicts all information contained to the -- contained in the documents referred to and the war log which the commander of the 9th VPS had access to. Likewise, the same applies to the report that he sent to Admiral Brovet on the 9th of December. Based on the documents that I have referred to, it is clear that the commander of the 9th VPS was kept up to date and knew exactly what was going on throughout the units under his command. It is also clear that he had full communication with Minister Rudolf and the Dubrovnik side. When these facts are complemented by witness testimonies that I have -- those witness testimonies that I have already referred to, then all of Jokic's allegations concerning the attack on Srdj on the 6th of December must be denied. He was merely trying to diminish his own responsibility and accuse other people of those developments in an unfounded way; that's shifting his own responsibility on to other people. It is quite illogical that because of an alleged willful attack by the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade Jokic should not have removed him or indeed do anything to have him removed. And yet, he sends Colonel Kovacevic over directly to have the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade removed at the same time. Had it been the case, namely, that a willful attack had taken place against Srdj there would Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond have been a great difference in terms of the responsibility of the respective commanders of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade and the commander of the 5th Brigade. In that situation, in order to keep the supreme command happy as long as the Croatian side, he decided to sacrifice the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade and had him removed swiftly. This was an easier step for him to take because this person was a fresh commander who had just arrived as replacement for the temporarily absent Commander Zdravkovic prior to the attack on Srdj. It would have been much more difficult if not actually impossible to remove the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade who had been around for a while and was a familiar face to the soldiers. They knew that an operation against Srdj had been approved, and people at the command of the VPS were bitter about the fact that they were denied support from 130-millimetre guns, and they believed this was the cause of the casualties that they suffered. When asked a logical question about why he did not remove the commander of the 3rd Battalion, Kovacevic, if this man had launched a willful attack, Jokic tried to justify this by saying that he never saw him again after the 6th of December, that he was not in his unit, and that he enjoyed the protection from high-ranking officers, the protection of high-ranking officers. However, other witnesses have stated that Captain Kovacevic was in his unit at the time. Finally, we could say that it was only easy to understand that Jokic would have been interested in being himself in charge of the investigation and to the events on the 6th of December because this would have positioned him well to manipulate information and evade his share in the responsibility of what happened on the 6th. His manipulation of the facts and information and the fact that he reported falsely to the supreme command is clear when one considers the evidence in this case. It is absolutely impossible to link General Strugar in any way to the attack against Srdj on the 6th of December, nor has there been any evidence to suggest any such links. Likewise, General Strugar was sidelined from the investigation into the 6th of December as the supreme command had taken over the investigation directly through the commander of the 9th VPS. Finally, Your Honours, the Defence submits, based on the arguments that have been presented in our final brief and closing arguments, that the accused, General Strugar, is innocent of all the charges in the third amended indictment. We propose, Your Honours, that you acquit the accused, General Strugar. Your Honours, I would like to thank you for your attention, and I would like to thank all the participants in these proceedings, the Registrar, the interpreters, the technicians. Your Honours, I merely have one small request to make. This would be for our client, the accused, to briefly address the Trial Chamber for two minutes, if that can be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for 43 years and 9 months, I had been an officer of the JNA. Throughout those years of service, I behaved in an honourable way. I performed to the best of my abilities, and I only followed the dictate of my own conscience. I am a soldier, but I have never been a man who would resort to the use of force easily. As a soldier, I know better than most people what war means. In 1991, I tried as hard as I could to use my decisions and my own actions to reduce and minimise the horrors of war. I experienced war at an early age back in 1941, World War II, when I was still a child. I had taken an oath to my country as a military officer. I promised to defend my country, and I promised to serve my army faithfully. I never broke my word. I am genuinely sorry for all human casualties and for all the damage that was caused. I am genuinely sorry for all the victims, all the people who were killed in Dubrovnik, as well as for all those young soldiers who were killed on Srdj as well as in other areas and positions. I am sorry that I was unable to do anything to stop and prevent all that suffering. When the indictment against me was raised, the very next day I stated publicly that I was not guilty, saying also that I would go immediately and face the International Tribunal in order to prove my innocence. Here I am today, standing before you, Your Honours. I am still convinced that you will make a just and equitable ruling. I thank you very much for your attention, Your Honours. May I sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will give consideration to its --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will give consideration to its decision in this case which will be announced when it is ready. We would thank all those involved in the proceeding for their assistance. That concludes the hearing.
